title: [RFC]: KV cache grouping for hybrid models with speculative drafters
body:
**Status:** Draft · **PRs:** #58207 (group size), #58380 (prefer `BLHNC`, stacked on #58207)

## TL;DR

Speculative drafters on hybrid models add a small KV cache bucket of their own, which breaks vLLM's KV cache grouping heuristic in two ways:

- **Too many groups (Qwen3.5 / 3.6 + DFlash):** a one-layer drafter bucket forces **one group per layer**: Qwen3.5-27B goes from 4 to 70 groups (#49730), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 4 to 46. Each group rebuilds attention metadata every step, so DFlash loses much of its speedup; forcing fewer groups today costs KV cache capacity.
- **Full attention padding (MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash):** the 5-layer drafter bucket sets the group size, which doesn't divide the target's 9 full attention layers, so a full attention padding layer is allocated for the whole context (#58175).

A two-part proposal fixes both:

| part | problem | fix | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 · #58207** | small drafter buckets force per-layer KV groups, or full attn padding | pick the group size by worst-case padding **bytes**; `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` (default 3) | 46 → **17** groups, **+54%** tok/s @c=1, **+36%** @c=32 | 11 → **7** groups, no full attn padding, KV capacity 5.76M → 5.96M |
| **2 · #58380** | `LBHNC` forces padding when drafter bytes/token ≠ target's | prefer `BLHNC` when the backends can run it and it avoids full attn padding or needs fewer groups | **5** groups, no padding, 7.53M tokens (> main's 7.42M); Triton only today | stays `LBHNC` at 7 groups (`BLHNC` would need 12 and has no full attn padding to remove) |

The parts are complementary: part 2 picks the path; part 1 is the fallback path (§5).

---

## 1. Background

**Motivation.** Enabling DFlash on Qwen3.5-27B raises the number of KV cache groups from 4 to **70**. Without a drafter, its 64 layers (48 GDN + 16 full attention) form 4 groups of 16; with DFlash, every layer gets its own group (64 target + 6 drafter). The drafter adds a one-layer full attention bucket, and the grouping heuristic falls back to one group per layer (#49730). Every group rebuilds its attention metadata each step, and GDN (linear attention) metadata builders are expensive, so this becomes per-step host overhead and DFlash runs well below its expected speedup; the effect is larger on Qwen3.5-4B. Forcing a larger group size recovers the throughput but, with today's grouping, costs KV cache capacity.

A drafter can also cost KV cache capacity rather than speed. MiMo-V2.5 + its DFlash drafter has buckets `[9 full, 39 SW, 5 drafter SW]`: the drafter bucket is the smallest, so the group size becomes 5, and the 9 full attention layers get a padding layer that grows with context (#58175 reports ~10% more KV capacity once it's removed).

Related reports:

| report | model | groups | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| #49730 | Qwen3.5-27B / 4B + DFlash (H100) | 4 without DFlash → 70 with (one per layer) | DFlash ITL much slower than expected; forcing gs=16 recovers ~10% tok/s on 27B but shrinks KV capacity 216k → 141k tokens |
| #51742 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (H200) | 46 | `build_attn_metadata` ~31 ms/step vs ~6 ms at 10 groups; output tok/s ~2× at c=1 with fewer groups |
| #52297 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | — | one GDN `build()` takes ~900 µs and is repeated per group |
| #58175 | MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash | 11 | 1 full attn padding layer; removing it gives +10.57% KV capacity (their setup); +8.4% in ours (5.76M → 6.25M) |
| #42505, #46462 | Qwen3.5 / 3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | — | DFlash slower than expected / than baseline at higher concurrency; not root-caused, likely related |

This RFC's own measurement (§4.1): Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash on B300 goes from 460 → 733 tok/s at c=1 when the 46 groups drop to 17.

### 1.0 Terms

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| bucket | all layers whose KV cache specs merge (same attention type and shape) |
| group / `group_size` (gs) | a KV cache group shares one block table; buckets are split into groups of `group_size` layers |
| page | one layer's slice of a block; its size is that layer's bytes/token × block size |
| padding | layer slots in a group with no layer behind them; allocated but never written |
| manager vs kernel block | the KV manager allocates *manager* blocks; attention kernels may need them split into smaller *kernel* blocks |
| `LBHNC` | layer-outermost `KVCacheLayout` (today's default): every page is resized to one size, each group gets `group_size` pages per block |
| `BLHNC` | block-outermost `KVCacheLayout`: a block is one contiguous run of per-layer pages, so pages of different sizes share a block. `LBNHC`/`BLNHC` group the same way as `LBHNC`/`BLHNC` |

### 1.1 Buckets, groups, padding

```
Legend:  F/f = target/DRAFTER full attn   S/s = target/DRAFTER sliding window   M = mamba/GDN
         ▓ = full attn padding (grows with context, up to max_model_len)
         ░ = SW / mamba padding or idle page (bounded by window / state)

drafter full-attn group, group_size = 5 (one physical block):
│ f │ ▓ │ ▓ │ ▓ │ ▓ │   4 of 5 pages never written

every group's block has the same byte size (block IDs are shared across groups)
```

| cost | grows with | note |
|---|---|---|
| per-step metadata | # groups | one block table + builder call per group; GDN builders are expensive |
| KV capacity | padded slots × bytes/request | full attn slot: up to `max_model_len` tokens; SW / mamba slot: bounded |

### 1.2 Bad cases

```python
group_size = min(bucket sizes)                       # main
if max(bucket sizes) < 1.5 * min(bucket sizes):
    group_size = max(bucket sizes)
```

The heuristic sizes groups from bucket **counts** only. A drafter adds a small bucket of its own, which breaks it in two ways. Each group is drawn as `[ ]` with one letter per layer slot.

#### Case 1: Qwen3.5 / 3.6 + DFlash: a one-layer drafter bucket forces one group per layer

Qwen3.5-27B + DFlash (4 → 70 groups), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (4 → 46), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B + Eagle3 (4 → 41). Per-step metadata overhead grows with the layer count.

```
Qwen3.6 alone:     buckets [30 M, 10 F]              gs = 10  →  4 groups
Qwen3.6 + DFlash:  buckets [30 M, 10 F, 5 s, 1 f]    gs = min(30, 10, 5, 1) = 1

bucket                   layers   groups on main (one layer each)
target mamba/GDN    M      30     [M][M][M][M][M][M][M][M][M][M] … [M]   30
target full attn    F      10     [F][F][F][F][F][F][F][F][F][F]         10
drafter SW          s       5     [s][s][s][s][s]                         5
drafter full attn   f       1     [f]   ← smallest bucket sets gs = 1     1
                                                                        ────
                                        metadata builds per step:        46
```

With #58207: Qwen3.6 + DFlash 17 groups, Qwen3.5 + Eagle3 9 groups.

#### Case 2: MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash: the drafter's bucket doesn't divide the target's

MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash. The 5-layer drafter bucket is the smallest, so it sets gs=5, and the 9 full attention layers get a padding slot that grows with context.

Why full attention padding is the one that matters: a padding slot costs whatever a real layer of that type would hold for each request.

| padding slot | holds per request | MiMo-V2.5, per slot |
|---|---|---|
| full attention | every token of the context | 2.5 KiB/token × 256k tokens ≈ **640 MiB** (≈ 2.5 GiB at 1M) |
| sliding window | only the window (128 tokens), plus tokens in flight | 5 KiB/token × 128 ≈ **0.6 MiB** (≈ 41 MiB worst case with 8k in-flight tokens) |

So one full attention padding slot wastes as much as hundreds of sliding-window slots, and it keeps growing with context length.

```
main    gs = 5 → 11 groups
  F  [FFFFF][FFFF▓]              ← full attn padding
  S  [SSSSS] ×7 + [SSSS░]
  s  [sssss]

#58207  gs = 9 → 7 groups
  F  [FFFFFFFFF]                 ← no full attn padding
  S  [SSSSSSSS░] ×4 + [SSSSSSS░░]
  s  [sssss░░░░]
```

---

## 2. Part 1 · #58207: group size by worst-case padding bytes

Replace the [min / 1.5×-max heuristic](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b3a87b2d04e6439e2a1aef0cbf9ca65328076c86/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py#L1547-L1558) with a search over group sizes that minimizes **worst-case padding bytes** per request, bounded below so groups can't explode:

```python
lo = max(smallest bucket, min(min_kv_cache_group_layers, largest bucket))
group_size = argmin over gs in [lo, largest bucket] of
    (Σ padding_slots(bucket, gs) × spec.max_memory_usage_bytes(vllm_config), num_groups(gs))
```

Padding is costed in bytes, so full attention padding (which grows with `max_model_len`) is avoided in favor of bounded sliding-window / mamba padding. The lower bound keeps groups from exploding: never below the smallest bucket, and never below `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` (default 3), so a one-layer drafter bucket can't force one group per layer.

```
Qwen3.6 + DFlash, gs = 3 → 17 groups (each bucket padded independently)
  M  [MMM] ×10    F  [FFF][FFF][FF▓][FF▓]    s  [sss][ss░]    f  [f▓▓]
```

## 3. Part 2 · #58380: prefer `BLHNC`

In `BLHNC` a block is one contiguous run of per-layer pages, so pages of different sizes share a block instead of being padded to one size. The widest non-state bucket sets the block; mamba / SW groups split to fit it. #58380 prefers these layouts when specs have mixed page sizes **and** every backend runs each attention block unsplit, since packed blocks can't be split into smaller kernel blocks:

| backend (B300) | kernel block sizes | can use `BLHNC` |
|---|---|---|
| Triton | any multiple of 16 | yes |
| FlashInfer | 16 / 32 / 64 | no |
| FlashAttention hd256 (FA4) | 128 | no |

**`BLHNC` cost check:** `BLHNC` is not always better (MiMo below: 7 → 12 groups), so #58380 also computes both groupings from the specs and picks `BLHNC` only if the `LBHNC` grouping would pad full attention, or `BLHNC` needs fewer groups.

Each row below is a separate group; rows align because every block is the same size:

```
Qwen3.6 + DFlash: 5 groups, 12-page blocks
full-attn ×1   │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │   f   │   10 target + drafter (2 pages): no padding
mamba ×3       │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ ░ │ ░ │   10 GDN states each, 2 idle pages
drafter sw ×1  │   s   │   s   │   s   │   s   │   s   │ ░ │ ░ │   5 layers × 2 pages, 2 idle pages

MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash under `BLHNC` (not picked by the cost check): 12 groups, 9-page blocks
full-attn ×1   │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │   9 full pages: no padding
SWA ×10        │   S   │   S   │   S   │   S   │ ░ │   4 layers × 2 pages, 1 idle page (one group has 3)
drafter SW ×1  │  d d d d d  (1.6 pages each)  │ ░ │   5 layers × 64 KiB = 8 pages, 1 idle page
```

## 4. Results by model and layout

### 4.1 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (1× B300)

| plan | groups | padding / request @256k | KV capacity | tok/s c=1 / c=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 46 | 0 | 7.42M | 460 / 4654 |
| #58207 | 17 | 3.05 GiB (full attn) | 5.19M | 733 / 6495 |
| **#58380** (Triton, `BLHNC`) | **5** | **58 MiB** | **7.53M** | **746 / 7463** |

### 4.2 MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash (TP2)

| plan | groups | padding / request @256k | KV capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 11 | 726 MiB (incl. 1 full attn layer) | 5.76M |
| #58175 | 18 | **90 MiB** | **6.25M** |
| #58207 | **7** | 469 MiB | 5.96M |
| `BLHNC` (#58380 doesn't pick it) | 12 | 266 MiB | 6.10M |

Padding is worst case (8192 in-flight tokens). Full attn padding grows with context, so `BLHNC` wins outright for Qwen3.6; MiMo has none, so it's a trade between groups and bounded bytes.

### 4.3 Qwen3.6 + DFlash: `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` sweep

![min-kv-cache-group-layers sweep](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LucasWilkinson/vllm/af4013a3827d250b266c6e48b1fc124880523780/pareto_min_layers.png)

| `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` | gs | groups | KV capacity | padding/req @256k | c=1 | c=32 | with #52297 ² c=1 / c=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (= main) | 1 | 46 | 7.42M | 0 | 460 | 4654 | 653 / 5735 |
| 2 | 2 | 24 | 6.42M | 1.02 GiB (+17%) | 684 | 5711 | 716 / 6247 |
| **3 (default)** | 3 | 17 | 5.19M | 3.02 GiB (+50%) | 710 | 6339 | 727 / 7100 |
| 4 | 5 | 10 | 4.80M | 4 GiB (+67%) | 726 | 6676 | 758 / 6865 |

² #52297 (open PR) computes GDN attention metadata once per step instead of per group, making extra groups cheaper.

### 4.4 Qwen3.6 + DFlash: `BLHNC` vs `LBHNC`

![BLHNC vs LBHNC](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LucasWilkinson/vllm/f52d0d4bb0b941fff5dbc5834f62d865db084188/pareto_packed.png)

## 5. How the two parts fit together

**Defaults after both PRs merge** (default backends, no `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT`). Padding is per request at 256k context (worst case, 8192 in-flight tokens):

| model (B300 backend) | main today | after #58207 + #58380 |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6 + DFlash (FlashInfer/FA) | `LBHNC`, 46 groups, no padding | `LBHNC`, **17** groups, 3.05 GiB padding (full attn) |
| Qwen3.6 + DFlash (`--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`) | `LBHNC`, 46 groups, no padding | **`BLHNC`, 5** groups, 58 MiB padding |
| MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash (FA) | `LBHNC`, 11 groups, 726 MiB padding (640 MiB full attn) | `LBHNC`, **7** groups, 469 MiB padding (no full attn) |
| MiMo-V2.6 + MTP (FA) | `LBHNC`, 6 groups, 203 MiB padding (SW) | unchanged |
| Qwen3.5 + Eagle3 (FlashInfer/FA) | `LBHNC`, 41 groups, no padding | `LBHNC`, 9 groups, 4 drafter full attn padding slots |
| single page size (Gemma3, gpt-oss, Llama4, Qwen3.5, …) | unchanged | unchanged |

**Recommendation:** land #58207 first (helps every layout/backend), then #58380. `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT` / connector preferences still win.

---

## 6. Alternatives considered

Other open PRs that change this heuristic, and what each gives for Qwen3.6 + DFlash:

| PR | approach | Qwen3.6 + DFlash | shortcoming |
|---|---|---|---|
| #51742 | ignore one-layer buckets when taking the min | gs=5, 10 groups | pads the drafter's full attn layer with 4 slots that grow with context |
| #58175 | shrink gs to a divisor of the full attn bucket sizes (targets MiMo) | gs=1, 46 groups | doesn't help drafters |
| #49472 | minimize padding + number of groups, counted in layers | gs=5, 10 groups | a padded full attn layer counts the same as a sliding-window one, so it pads full attn |

Other approaches:

- **Bigger `block_size` for the lone drafter group** (same bytes, fewer layers): prefix-cache hits align to the LCM of group block sizes, so hits get ~5× coarser for every group.
- **Only forbid one layer per group (`group_size ≥ 2`) and minimize padding:** still 24 groups for Qwen3.6 + DFlash, and over-splits models with cheap padding (Gemma3-27B 7 → 31 groups).
- **Absolute cap on the number of groups:** the right cap depends on the backend (GDN vs FlashAttention metadata cost).
- **Drafter-aware sizing** (size groups from target buckets, pad the drafter): worst case when the drafter has a full attention layer, and drafter layers can only be identified heuristically at grouping time.
- **Separate KV pool for drafter layers:** removes the constraint entirely, but is a much larger allocator change.
- **#58345 (rescale sliding-window blocks for `BLHNC`):** on main (since #53007) sliding-window layers already use the full attention block size when the backend allows it (group block sizes 262144 ×3, 592, 592); when it doesn't, rescaling would need kernel-block splitting, which `BLHNC` can't do.

---

## 7. Open questions

1. **Default `--min-kv-cache-group-layers`:** 3 (17 groups, −30% KV capacity on Qwen3.6 + DFlash) or 4 (10 groups, +2–5% tok/s, −35%)? Should it depend on whether the model has GDN layers?
2. **`BLHNC` with FlashInfer / FlashAttention:** re-page inside the kernels (as #55219 / #57169 do for sparse MLA), or stop inflating the block size for block-outermost layouts (but then few GDN states fit per block)?
3. **FlashAttention drafter block size:** the 128-only FA4 hd256 kernel block is derived from the *target's* head size and applied to a hd128 drafter, causing `No common block size for 592` on main unless `--block-size 128` is set. Separate fix.
4. **Validation:** #58380 switches mixed-page-size models to `BLHNC` when the cost check passes on capable backends; needs accuracy and throughput validation beyond DFlash and MiMo.

---

## 8. Methodology

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 --max-num-seqs 32 --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 128 \
  --mamba-cache-dtype bfloat16 --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16 [--min-kv-cache-group-layers N] \
  [--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN] \
  --speculative-config '{"model":"z-lab/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash","method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7}'
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 --dataset-name hf --dataset-path openai/gsm8k --hf-split test \
  --num-prompts max(32, 8*C) --max-concurrency C --num-warmups 2*C
```

| item | value |
|---|---|
| hardware | 1× B300 per run (MiMo: TP2, `max_model_len` 1M) |
| runs | single; noise ~2–3% (repeated gs=5) |
| interactivity | 1000 / p99 TPOT |
| acceptance length | 5.1–5.2 in all Qwen runs |
| `--block-size 128` | needed on all variants, including main: FlashAttention's 128-only FA4 hd256 kernel block is derived from the target's head size and also applied to the hd128 drafter, which otherwise fails with `No common block size for 592` |


---

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to run the experiments and draft this RFC; I have reviewed its contents.

title: [RFC]: Hardening /v1/messages (Anthropic API) for Claude Code across model families
body:
### Motivation

Claude Code can run against vLLM through the Anthropic Messages endpoint (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` → `/v1/messages`). Claude Code's agentic loop is a demanding client of that endpoint:

- It sends every request with ~25 tools, many with large nested JSON schemas.
- It uses interleaved thinking with parallel tool calls.
- It sends inline `role: "system"` messages that change every turn.
- It sends side queries (title generation, the auto-mode permission classifier) with `stop_sequences` and small `max_tokens` budgets.
- It recovers from context overflow based on the error it gets back.

This issue audits the current converter (`vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/`) and the HF chat templates of the major open model families against real Claude Code traffic. We found:

- several gaps that affect every model family;
- a set of model-specific breakages, some of which return **400 on Claude Code's default requests**.

Many of the small fixes already have open PRs, often more than one per problem. This issue gathers them so they can be deduplicated and prioritized, and it proposes the pieces that have no owner yet.

**How we checked**

- We captured `/v1/messages` traffic from Claude Code 2.1.281 through a logging proxy (~50 requests covering main-loop turns, title generation and the auto-mode classifier).
- We replayed synthetic Claude Code-shaped conversations through `AnthropicServingMessages.to_chat_completion_request` → `chat_utils` post-processing.
- We rendered the result with the current HF templates, and with `mistral_common` / the DeepSeek Python encoders / Harmony where applicable.

Items marked *(unverified)* were not reproduced at runtime.

**Observed request shape (from captures)**

| Field | Values seen |
|---|---|
| `system` | List of text blocks with `cache_control`. The first is the `x-anthropic-billing-header` line. |
| `messages` | Contains inline `role: "system"` messages at non-leading positions (e.g. a `<total_tokens>` update each turn). |
| `thinking` | `{"type":"adaptive"}`, `{"type":"adaptive","display":"omitted"}`, `{"type":"enabled"}`, `{"type":"disabled"}`, or absent |
| `output_config` | `{"effort":"high"}`; title generation adds `format: json_schema` |
| `context_management` | `{"edits":[{"type":"clear_thinking_20251015","keep":"all"}]}` |
| `max_tokens` | `32000` (main loop), `2112` (classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]`), `64` (stage-1 classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</severity>"]`) |
| `tool_result` | `is_error` is set on most results. Content is a string or a list of text/image blocks. User turns often carry extra text blocks (system reminders) after the tool results. |

---

### Part 1: Converter / API gaps (all models)

| # | Gap | Location | Impact | Existing work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Inline system messages are always hoisted into the leading system prompt.** `_detect_merge_inline_system` is called with the CLI `--chat-template` value, which is `None` by default, so it returns `True` for every deployment that uses the model's own template. Claude Code sends a changing inline system message every turn, so the leading system text changes every request. | `serving.py:142,152,248-257` | **Prefix cache misses on the whole conversation, every turn.** Also changes semantics: mid-conversation instructions become part of the global system prompt. | #53393, #48874, #41114, #46710; PRs #53501, #56520, #52978, #47681 (competing approaches) |
| 2 | **The `thinking` request field is silently dropped.** `AnthropicMessagesRequest` has no `thinking` field and pydantic ignores extras. `output_config.effort` → `reasoning_effort` then forces `enable_thinking=True` (`chat_completion/protocol.py:585`). Anthropic's default when `thinking` is absent is *off*, but we use the template default, which is usually *on*. | `protocol.py:121` | Side queries (title generation, classifier) reason and spend their `max_tokens` budget before answering. `display: "omitted"` is ignored. | PRs #58613, #53058 |
| 3 | **Stop strings are matched against reasoning text.** `check_stop_strings` runs over the full detokenized output. | `v1/engine/detokenizer.py:130` | The classifier's `</block>` / `</severity>` can match inside `<think>` and end the request with no verdict. | #51669 (related) |
| 4 | **Context-overflow errors are not in Anthropic's format.** vLLM returns "This model's maximum context length is …". Claude Code decides whether to auto-compact or retry with a smaller `max_tokens` based on Anthropic's context-limit error messages *(exact strings unverified)*. Claude Code always sends `max_tokens=32000`, so a 128k-context deployment rejects prompts once they pass ~99k tokens. | `renderers/params.py:357,499` | Long sessions fail hard instead of compacting. | none found |
| 5 | **Unknown content-block types reject the whole request (422).** `AnthropicContentBlock.type` is a closed `Literal`. `document` (PDFs from the Read tool), `search_result`, `tool_addition` / `tool_removal` and server-tool blocks all fail. Once one is in the history, every later request in the session fails. | `protocol.py:41` | Session becomes unrecoverable. | #57324, #46790; PRs #45653, #57693, #46797, #47747, #47877 |
| 6 | **Images in a `tool_result` become a separate `user` message** inserted between tool messages. | `serving.py:445-455` | Gemma 4 silently drops later tool results. Mistral returns 400 (`Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user'`). DeepSeek-V3.2 raises. MiniMax-M3 and Gemma 4 could render the image inside the tool message natively. | none found |
| 7 | **`tool_reference` produces an extra tool message, and the first one is empty.** | `serving.py:457-465` | 400 on Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 (`Unexpected item type in content`) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (`No tool calls but found tool output`). Python repr rendered on MiniMax. | #52489; PRs #52498, #52610 |
| 8 | **User text after `tool_result`s in the same turn becomes a separate trailing `user` message.** Templates that keep reasoning only after the last user message then drop the current tool loop's reasoning. | `serving.py:306` | Interleaved thinking lost mid-loop on GLM-4.7/5/5.1/5.2, Qwen3.5/3.6, MiniMax-M2.x and DeepSeek-V3.2. | none found |
| 9 | **`is_error` on `tool_result` is dropped.** | `serving.py:408-445` | The model cannot tell failed tool calls from successful ones. | none found |
| 10 | **System blocks are joined with `""`.** | `serving.py:257` | Prompt text runs together, e.g. `…for Claude.You are…`. | none found |
| 11 | **Malformed tool-call arguments crash non-streaming** (`json.loads` → 500). | `serving.py` (`messages_full_converter`) | Hard failure on a single bad generation. | PRs #57244, #52519 |
| 12 | **Error envelopes and types don't match Anthropic's.** FastAPI 422s are not wrapped in Anthropic's error format. Stream errors use `internal_error` instead of `api_error` / `overloaded_error`. Mid-stream upstream errors are replaced with "Invalid data format received". | `api_router.py`, `serving.py` | Client retry/backoff logic doesn't fire correctly. | PRs #58023, #46162 |
| 13 | **`x-api-key` is not accepted** by `--api-key` auth. | `serve/middleware/authenticate.py` | Requires `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` instead of `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. | PRs #51675, #51588 |
| 14 | **No `ping` or early `message_start` during long prefills** (100k+ token prompts). | `serving.py` (`message_stream_converter`) | Idle-timeout risk through proxies and load balancers *(unverified)*. | none found |
| 15 | **Tool-call id collisions/format.** vLLM-generated ids are reused across turns for some parsers (e.g. Kimi `functions.X:0`). | | See Kimi below. | PR #35667 |

---

### Part 2: Model / template-specific findings

The common thread: every family uses **different names and values** for thinking and effort. Examples: `enable_thinking`, `thinking`, `thinking_mode`, `low_effort`, `thinking_budget`, and effort sets such as `{low,high}`, `{none,high}` or `{xhigh,medium,low}`. Passing `output_config.effort` straight through as `reasoning_effort` therefore gives inconsistent behavior, and 400s on several families.

| Family | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3.8** (27B, Flash-Next, 2.4T) | The template raises `Unexpected reasoning effort high. Supported types are xhigh (default), medium, and low.` Claude Code sends `high` by default, so **every default Claude Code request returns 400**. 2.4T also raises `Disabling thinking is not supported.` | confirmed |
| **Qwen3.5 / 3.6** | Keep reasoning only after the last user message (item 8). 3.6 supports `preserve_thinking`, which vLLM never sets. The system-first guard is hidden only by item 1. | confirmed |
| **Qwen3.5 / Qwen3-Coder** | Historical arguments rendered with `\| string` produce Python `True`. Qwen3-Coder renders nested `anyOf` lossily. | confirmed (template-side) |
| **GLM-5.2 / 5.3** | Effort is mapped as `'high' if effort == 'high' else 'max'` (5.2), or only `{low,high}` is recognized (5.3), so `low`/`medium` become **Max**. 5.3 cannot disable thinking: the generation prompt is always `<think>`. `glm47_moe` parser switches to content-only when `enable_thinking=False`, so a naive disabled-thinking mapping would leak reasoning into `content`. | confirmed |
| **MiniMax-M3** | The template's `thinking_mode` (`enabled`/`disabled`/`adaptive`) maps 1:1 to Anthropic `thinking.type`, but vLLM never sets it. The template has no branch for non-leading system messages, so they are silently dropped once item 1 is fixed. | confirmed |
| **MiniMax-M2.x** | Reasoning is dropped before the last user message (item 8). | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V3.1** | The stock HF template does `'<｜tool▁sep｜>' + arguments`, but `chat_utils` has already turned arguments into a dict, so rendering raises `TypeError` on any history containing a tool call. It also never renders `tools`. Workaround: `examples/tool_chat_template_deepseekv31.jinja`. | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V3.2** (encoder) | `drop_thinking = messages[-1]["role"] == "user"` drops the current loop's reasoning (item 8). The strict tool-ordering check breaks on items 6 and 7. A non-merged inline system message has no role token and lands inside `<think>`. | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1** | V4 is fine. V4.1 raises on `effort: "medium"` (accepts low/high/xhigh/max). | confirmed |
| **Kimi K2-Thinking / K2.5 / K2.6** | The template renders only the tool-call **id**, never the tool name (`<\|tool_call_begin\|>{{ id }}`). Any id not generated by Kimi on vLLM (`toolu_…`, `chatcmpl-tool-…`, after `/model` or a resumed session) loses the tool name. Thinking uses `thinking`, not `enable_thinking`. | confirmed |
| **Kimi K3** | Only low/high/max effort are accepted, so `medium` / `xhigh` return 400. Tool-result matching is robust to foreign ids. | confirmed |
| **gpt-oss (Harmony)** | `max` / `xhigh` effort raise. Reasoning cannot be disabled. Images are dropped. Each inline system message becomes a new developer message. JSON Schema → TypeScript is lossy: `anyOf`+enum, `allOf`, `$ref` and `const` become `any`, and `additionalProperties` maps become `{}` (affects Claude Code's `AskUserQuestion` / `Workflow` tools). | confirmed |
| **Mistral / Devstral** | `validate_request_params` allows only `{none, high}` effort, so Claude Code's other values return 400. Devstral-Small-2 and Devstral-2 raise `think tokens are not available for this tokenizer` whenever the history contains a thinking block. `truncate_tool_call_ids` works but logs a WARNING per historical tool call on every request. | confirmed |
| **Gemma 4** | Later tool results are lost when a user message is inserted (item 6). The template renders `anyOf` as an empty type, renders enums only for strings, and renders map-typed objects as fake properties (hits `AskUserQuestion`). | confirmed |
| **Nemotron v3** | The template reads `low_effort`, which vLLM never sets, so effort has no effect. Thinking cannot be disabled via the Anthropic API. | confirmed |
| **Seed-OSS** | Thinking is controlled only by `thinking_budget` (default unlimited). The default tool rendering is Python signatures that drop nested types and enums; `use_json_tooldef` fixes this but is off by default. Historical arguments use Python repr. | confirmed |

---

### Proposed Change

Suggested priority order:

1. **Per-model thinking/effort mapping layer.** Map Anthropic `thinking.type` (+ `budget_tokens`) and `output_config.effort` onto each model's native switch (`enable_thinking`, `thinking`, `thinking_mode`, `low_effort`, `thinking_budget`) and clamp to the levels that model accepts. Treat absent `thinking` as disabled only where the model can actually disable it. This extends #58613 and #52738, and removes most of the 400s above.
2. **Inline system handling that preserves the prefix.** Keep inline system messages in place, or fold them into the adjacent user turn when the template requires system-first (as proposed in #53393). Never hoist them into the leading system block. Detect the template requirement against the *resolved* tokenizer template, not the CLI flag.
3. **Converter structure fixes.**
   - Keep tool-result images inside the `tool` message.
   - Emit one merged user message per Anthropic user turn, so the trailing text doesn't cut off reasoning.
   - Mark `is_error` (e.g. an `Error:` prefix).
   - Join system blocks with `\n\n`.
   - Emit a single `tool_reference` message.
4. **Error compatibility.**
   - Translate context-overflow errors to Anthropic's messages so Claude Code can auto-compact or reduce `max_tokens`.
   - Degrade unknown content blocks to text instead of failing with 422.
   - Use Anthropic error types and envelopes throughout.
5. **Model-specific fixes.**
   - Rewrite Kimi tool-call ids to `functions.{name}:{idx}`.
   - Drop historical reasoning for Mistral tokenizers without `[THINK]`.
   - Add a schema-normalization pass (flatten `anyOf`/`$ref`) for Harmony, Gemma 4 and Seed-OSS.
   - Evaluate stop strings against content only, not reasoning.
6. **Regression coverage.** Add a small Claude Code-shaped fixture (captured request shapes, no user content) to `tests/entrypoints/anthropic/`, rendered through the converter for each supported template family.

### Feedback Period

~2 weeks.

### CC List

_No response_

### Any Other Things

AI assistance was used for this investigation (Claude Code): it analyzed the captured traffic, read the converter code and rendered templates across model families. File/line references are against `main` at e33de821c0.

### Describe the bug On Model Runner V1 with speculative decoding, a `thinking_token_budget` that forces a multi-token `reasoning_end_str` often emits the end sequence wrong: end tokens go missing with one of the model's own tokens in their place, and some reasoning sections never close. On main `9f07d023d07f`, 17 of 32 budget-forced ends were corrupted. The same arm on Model Runner V2 was 0 of 32. The cause is in `ThinkingBudgetStateHolder._update_think_state` (`vllm/v1/sample/thinking_budget_state.py`, added with #34668). While forcing, it advances through the end sequence on the step's draft tokens rather than on accepted tokens, and forces only one position per step. V2 forces every position of the verification window. The fix is in #52677 (`df93fe6c67`), because that PR forces the same end sequence through the same state machine. #### Reproduction One GB10 (sm_121), main `9f07d023d07f` (precompiled wheel `0.30.1rc1.dev20+g9f07d023d`), torch 2.13.0+cu130, driver 580.173.02, Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 with its MTP head. ``` VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"qwen3_5_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3,"max_model_len":262144}' \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --reasoning-config '{"reasoning_end_str":"I have to give the solution based on the reasoning directly now."}' \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 --max-num-seqs 32 --max-model-len 262144 \ --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --long-prefill-token-threshold 7840 ``` (plus YaRN `hf-overrides`, the `qwen3_coder` tool parser, and `enable_thinking: false` in the default chat template kwargs) Client: `/v1/chat/completions`, `temperature` 0.7, `reasoning_effort` "xhigh", `thinking_token_budget` 256, `max_tokens` 2048. Two prompts that make the model reason at length (write a fixed line 150 or 250 times in its reasoning, then answer "done" or "prime"), 16 requests each at concurrency 16. `reasoning_end_str` is 14 tokens. The budget fired on all 32. | end sequence | reasoning closed | final answer followed | requests | |---|---|---|---| | intact | yes | yes | 14 | | intact | yes | no, the answer re-entered the loop | 1 | | corrupted | yes | yes | 7 | | corrupted | yes | no, the answer re-entered the loop | 5 | | corrupted | no, reasoning ran to `max_tokens` | no | 5 | | **total** | 27 of 32 closed | 21 of 32 answered | 15 intact, **17 corrupted** | "Intact" means the reasoning ends with the phrase exactly once. What the corrupted ones look like: ``` ...I have the solution based on the reasoning directly now. ...I have to give final based on the analysis now. ...I have to give final based on this directly now. ...I need give the solution based on the reasoning directly now. ...I have considered the solution based on the reasoning directly now. ...I have already the solution based on the reasoning directly now. ``` Same host, model, flags, prompts, budget and client: | run | budget fired | intact | corrupted | closed | final answer | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | main `9f07d023d07f`, V1 | 32 | 15 | **17** | 27 | 21 | | main `9f07d023d07f`, V2 (`Using V2 Model Runner` in the log) | 32 | 32 | 0 | 32 | 25 | | #52677 `df93fe6c67`, V1 | 32 | 32 | 0 | 32 | 26 | Fisher two-sided p = 8.2e-7 for corrupted, main V1 against #52677. The #52677 row is that PR's tree on its own wheel (base `f944491db9`), so it differs from main in more than this fix; the V2 row is main itself. The requests without a final answer in the two clean rows closed intact and then repeated the prompt's line in the answer, which is the prompt doing its job. #### Mechanism (main `9f07d023d07f`) When the budget runs out, lines 422-445 force the first end token at one position (`force_index = [remaining_budget]`, `[0]` or `[spec_len]`). On later steps, lines 447-478 walk `spec_token_ids`: a draft equal to the next end token advances `end_count` and its position is left unforced, and only the first non-matching position (or the bonus slot) is forced. At a matching position the target decides on its own logits. If it samples something else, the matching draft is rejected and the target's token is committed, but `end_count` has already moved past it, so the next step forces from a later index: ``` accepted so far END[0..3] drafts [END[4], x, y] -> end_count 3 -> 5; force position 1 := END[5] position 0 not forced; the target samples T instead of END[4]; T is committed next step forcing resumes at END[6]; END[4] and END[5] are never emitted ``` That is the "I have to give final based on ..." shape above: " final" where " the solution" belongs. Two more cases come from the same walk: - when the drafts reach the last end token, `in_end` is cleared before any of them is verified; - when the transition forces the first end token part-way through the window and the draft there matches it, the positions after it go unforced. #### Unit tests `tests/v1/sample/test_thinking_forced_end_spec.py` (in #52677) drives the holder in the order V1 calls it (bonus pass in `Sampler`, target pass in `RejectionSampler`) with greedy verification, CPU only. Against the unfixed code, 5 of its 6 cases fail: | case | unfixed | fixed | |---|---|---| | thinking budget, target rejects a matching draft | FAIL, emits `[40, 41, 42, 77, 200]` for `[40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 200]` | pass | | thinking budget, forcing starts inside the draft window | FAIL, emits `[40, 77, 41, ...]` | pass | | loop break (#52677), target rejects a matching draft | FAIL, same shape | pass | | loop break (#52677), ramp release runs out | FAIL, same shape | pass | | loop break (#52677), drafts reach the last end token | FAIL, the sequence restarts at token 0 | pass | | control, no draft ever matches | pass | pass | #### The fix in #52677 - progress through the end sequence comes from the accepted output; - every position of the verification window, drafts and bonus, is forced to its own end token; - that includes forcing that starts part-way through a window: the budget transition, the loop-break fire, and the ramp release running out. One runtime file, `vllm/v1/sample/thinking_budget_state.py`, plus the test file. Through #52677's loop breaking, which forces the same end sequence when it detects a repeating reasoning loop (same settings except loop breaking on at 128/4/4 with a 256-token floor, `thinking_token_budget` 32768 so only the loop breaker fires, `max_tokens` 4096): | V1 unless stated | host | code | forced ends | corrupted | never closed | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | without the fix, two runs | spark-6 | `351f7b2c5e` | 51 | 23 | 8 | | an earlier version of the fix | spark-6 | on `351f7b2c5e` | 24 | 0 | 0 | | without the fix | spark-5 | `a650585283` | 25 | 6 | 2 | | with the fix | spark-5 | `df93fe6c67` | 25 | 0 | 0 | | with the fix, V2 | spark-5 | `df93fe6c67` | 24 | 0 | 0 | On spark-5 the two V1 rows are one commit apart: 6 of 25 against 0 of 25, Fisher p = 0.022. Matching fires by the scheduler log's request ID instead of by the phrase gives 7 of 26 against 0 of 25 (p = 0.0098), because one unfixed request lost the phrase's tail too. The unfixed rate differs between the hosts (23 of 51 against 6 of 25) at different commits with one or two runs each, so I would not read anything into that gap. #### Limits - V1 only. V2 is the default runner from v0.29.0 (#53183), and main on V2 was clean in the same arm. - One model, one phrase, one GPU type, n = 32 per row. A forced end is corrupted only when the model disagrees with a correct draft inside the end sequence, so the rate depends on the model, the phrase and the temperature. At temperature 0 on the same model, a separate run saw no corruption in 297 such positions. - In spec mode, when a batch has no drafts at all and V1 uses the plain sampler, the holder's row layout gives each request zero rows. That predates this and is not addressed here. #### Related, and why this is not a duplicate - #39697, with open fixes #43210 and #53572: the holder misses a natural reasoning end when `reasoning_end_str` carries a transition phrase, and forces the phrase into the answer. Same file, different defect. Neither diff touches the draft walk at lines 447-478. - #58231: `thinking_token_budget` with speculative decoding and `top_p < 1` emits token id 0 instead of the forced end. Same configuration, different cause (split-row top-p masking in `topk_topp_triton.py`). The corruption here is real vocabulary, never token 0. Searched open and closed issues and PRs for `_update_think_state`, `ThinkingBudgetStateHolder`, `reasoning_end_str`, and "thinking budget" with speculative decoding / MTP / spec decode.

title: [Hybrid GDN] Explicit --block-size misaligned with mamba page makes SimpleCPU KV offload silently write-only; startup should reject or warn
body:
# Upstream issue draft（送 admin 过目版 v1，2026-09-24；联合署名 llm-1 & f280，admin 09-23 23:47Z 批）

> 投 vLLM GitHub issue 前的内部草稿。证据双方独立实测，可逐条复算。

---

**Title**: `[Hybrid GDN] Explicit --block-size misaligned with mamba page makes SimpleCPU KV offload silently write-only; startup should reject or warn`

## Summary

On hybrid GDN models (Qwen3.5/Qwen3.8 family, `linear_attention` + periodic `full_attention`), enabling the SimpleCPU KV offload connector (`VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD=1`) together with an **explicit** `--block-size` that does not match the mamba-page alignment results in the offload connector becoming **write-only**: blocks are stored to CPU (RSS grows, write path active) but the read path never serves a single token (`external_kv_transfer` stays 0, re-prefill after forced eviction costs the same as a cold prefill). Omitting `--block-size` (letting the engine auto-compute the aligned size) makes the same setup fully functional. The failure is **silent** — no error, no warning — and looks exactly like "offload enabled" from the outside.

## Environment (two independent deployments, same wheel)

- vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev400+g38537331d`; model Qwen3.8-27B W4A16 (AutoRound / AWQ-INT4), `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN: 48 GDN `linear_attention` + 16 `full_attention` (interval=4), mamba align, 1 MTP layer
- **Deployment A (llm-1)**: fp8 KV, MTP on, `gpu_memory_utilization=0.93`, `--kv-offloading-size 16` (GiB), mamba cache fp16
- **Deployment B (f280)**: fp8 KV, MTP on, `--kv-cache-memory 8105442816` (pool 208,005 tok), CPU offload 30 GB / 584 blocks, mamba cache fp32
- Both: `VLLM_USE_SIMPLE_KV_OFFLOAD=1`, prefix caching on, `max_model_len=131072`

> Note on version: filed against a dev build (`0.29.1rc1.dev400`) because both deployments run it in production; the same checks have **not** yet been run on a stable release. If the stable branch behaves differently we will report back.

## Symptom (deployment A, explicit `--block-size 128`)

- Startup log: `Setting attention block size to 896 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size` → `kv cache group sizes [896, 896, 896, 896]`
- Write path alive: connector RSS grows ~16 GiB under eviction pressure (all FA blocks)
- Read path dead: probe = T1 cold prefill of a 30k-token doc, T2 warm re-ask (local hit), force eviction with 6×35k-token filler docs, 75 s drain, T3 re-ask:
  - **T3/T1 = 1.006–1.46** (re-ask after eviction ≈ full cold prefill)
  - **Δ`prompt_tokens_by_source{external_kv_transfer}` = 0** across the T3 window
- No error/warning anywhere in logs.

## Fix-by-configuration (both deployments, read path fully functional)

Dropping the explicit flag → engine auto-computes the aligned block size:

| Deployment | Startup fingerprint | T3/T1 | Δ external_kv_transfer (T3 window) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A, `--block-size 128` | `[896×4]` | 1.006–1.46 | **0** |
| A, flag omitted | `Setting attention block size to 816` / `[816×4]` | **0.032 / 0.048** (two windows) | **+29,376** |
| B, flag omitted (fp32 mamba) | `Setting attention block size to 1584` / `[1584×4]` | **0.044** (re-run 0.0438; instrumented variant 0.1279) | **+28,512** |

Answers identical across T1/T2/T3 in all runs. The only changed variable between the broken and working rows on deployment A is the explicit `--block-size` flag (single-variable matrix over {mamba dtype, async_scheduling, cumem, block-size} — block-size was the only HIT).

## Expected behavior

When a hybrid-GDN model is configured with an explicit `--block-size` whose resulting attention page geometry is incompatible with the mamba page / offload connector granularity, vLLM should **refuse to start or at least emit a loud WARN**, instead of running silently with a write-only offload connector.

Suggested improvements (joint appendix):
1. **Startup validation**: reject or WARN when explicit `--block-size` conflicts with mamba-page alignment for hybrid models (the auto-align path `interface.py:918` already computes the correct value — the explicit-flag path appears to bypass the same protection, raising to a value (896) that satisfies the page-size inequality but breaks connector store/load granularity).
2. **Connector robustness**: SimpleCPU connector should detect the granularity mismatch and fail loudly rather than store-never-load.
3. **Observability**: expose store/load counter pairs in `/metrics` so "write-only offload" is directly visible (today only `external_kv_transfer` hits/queries tell the story indirectly).

## Notes

- Without KV offloading, the explicit `--block-size 128` is harmless: it is raised to 896 and never actually runs at 128 — inference correctness is unaffected. The bug only bites the offload read path.
- Reproduction probe and full datasets available on request (both deployments, archived JSON + logs).

*Joint report by the maintainers of two independent production deployments (anonymous), independent reproductions on an identical wheel build, 2026-09-24.*

title: [Bug] [watermarking]: reference detection server does not support dual_key_gumbel; detector alpha default disagrees with generation default
body:
### Your current environment

N/A — code-level report against current `main` (17e50b9b761023d5f2499f062507df1ff49092a4); no runtime environment involved.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Two related gaps after #56122.

### 1. Reference detection server cannot detect `dual_key_gumbel` output

`examples/basic/online_serving/watermark_detection_server.py` always constructs `GumbelWatermarkDetector` (line 60). Its argparse takes only `--tokenizer / --key / --prf / --context-width / --p-value-threshold`. There is no `--algorithm` or `--alpha`, so text generated with `algorithm="dual_key_gumbel"` cannot be detected with the reference server. `docs/features/watermarking.md` points users at this server as the deployment pattern (line 228). It should accept `--algorithm dual_key_gumbel --alpha <value>` and build `DualKeyGumbelWatermarkDetector`.

### 2. Detector `alpha` default disagrees with generation default

- `DualKeyGumbelWatermarkDetector.__init__` defaults `alpha=0.2` (`vllm/v1/watermarking/gumbel.py:220`)
- `WatermarkConfig.alpha` defaults to `0.1` (`vllm/config/watermarking.py:35`), as does `DualKeyGumbelWatermarker` (`gumbel.py:107`)

The detector uses `alpha` in the variance normalization (`gumbel.py:252`: `variance = (1 - self.alpha) ** 2 + self.alpha ** 2`), so a silent default mismatch changes p-values. Suggest aligning the detector default to 0.1, or dropping the default and requiring `alpha` explicitly.

### Docs nit

Worth a one-line note in the constraints section that `deduplicate_contexts` and speculative decoding are mutually exclusive in effect today. It is stated at `docs/features/watermarking.md:80-82`, but under the spec-decode heading where it is easy to miss.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] CLI configuration without runtime initialization
body:
# CLI configuration without runtime initialization Updated September 24. Code references use main `7a9406690ebe`. The CLI already gets types, defaults and help from config. The problem is that reading those definitions imports runtime code, and building the parser constructs config objects with platform-dependent defaults. Even `vllm --version` builds the serve parser first. I propose keeping the config classes and `get_kwargs`, while separating **describing arguments** from **constructing their values**. Build only the requested command's parser. For nested config defaults, use the existing JSON conversion path during parsing instead of constructing config to print help. Keep platform extensions before parsing, where they can still register flags. This replaces the generator and separate declaration layer from #56884. The intended result is a responsive CLI with fewer incidental imports. A serving-startup improvement would need a separate measurement. ## Current structure Config owns field definitions and validation. `get_kwargs()` derives argparse settings from those fields. Registration adds flag names, aliases and CLI overrides. `EngineArgs` receives the parsed values, resolves model- and hardware-dependent settings, and constructs runtime config. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Config fields"] -->|"types, defaults, docs"| K["get_kwargs"] K --> A["Argparse"] O["Flag names and
CLI overrides"] --> A A --> E["EngineArgs"] E -->|"resolve inputs"| R["Runtime config
and validation"] ``` `EngineArgs` mirrors fields and maps them back into config, but removing that repetition does not remove the import cost. [`get_kwargs`][kwargs] is already the connection between config and the parser. ### A scheduler option, end to end `--max-num-batched-tokens` has three different defaults for a reason: | Stage | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `SchedulerConfig` | Integer, default 2048, bound `ge=1`. Its docstring says the default is mainly for testing. | | CLI / `EngineArgs` | `None` means the user has not selected a value. An explicit value uses the human-readable integer converter. | | Engine configuration | Resolve an unset value using the device, serving/offline context and model settings; then construct `SchedulerConfig`. | For H100/H200-class GPUs, the initial choices are 8192 tokens for serving and 16384 for offline use, before further model-dependent adjustments. Replacing the CLI's `None` with the field's 2048 would change behavior. The parser also accepts zero; the `ge=1` check runs when `SchedulerConfig` is constructed. [Declaration][scheduler], [registration][scheduler-flags], [runtime defaults][batch-defaults]. ## Work that help triggers There are both import-time and parser-construction costs: ```mermaid flowchart TD S["CLI startup"] --> P["Package initialization"] P --> ENV["env_override"] --> T["Torch"] S --> CMD["Import commands;
build every parser"] CMD --> API["Serving implementation"] --> F["FastAPI"] CMD --> CFG["arg_utils / config imports"] CFG --> DEP["Torch, Transformers,
OpenAI"] CMD --> PARSE["Build serve arguments"] PARSE --> PL["Load general plugins"] PARSE --> HOOK["Platform hook
and device choices"] PARSE --> FACT["Construct config defaults"] FACT --> PLATFORM["Resolve current platform"] HOOK --> PLATFORM PLATFORM --> RT["Platform / backend imports"] ``` Importing `vllm.config.scheduler` still executes `vllm.config.__init__`. Both the package and individual config modules therefore need cheap imports. Some dependencies are small declarations stored in heavy packages; others are functions used only during runtime construction. Moving the declaration or importing the function at its use site removes the dependency without duplicating config. [Command loading][cli-main], [config exports][config-init], [one quantization import][quantization]. The parser adds two less obvious dependencies: - `_compute_kwargs()` visits every field and calls its default factory. A trace of ordinary top-level and serve help reached `DeviceConfig.__post_init__` and `CompilationConfig.__post_init__` through `get_kwargs(VllmConfig)`. - `AsyncEngineArgs.add_cli_args()` loads general plugins and calls `current_platform.pre_register_and_update(parser)`. Plugins can register types or flags. The choices for `--mm-processor-device` also read `current_platform.device_type`. Moving imports does not remove these calls. [Factories][kwargs], [plugin and platform hooks][async-args], [device choices][device-choices]. ### Why lazy field lookup is insufficient Skipping unused fields avoids constructing `DeviceConfig` for the aggregate config. But `--compilation-config` is an exposed field. Its factory still constructs `CompilationConfig`, whose post-init chooses a compile backend and applies Torch-version-dependent settings. The current help prints the resulting configuration, including those settings. [Flag registration][compilation-flag], [initialization][compilation-init]. The observed path is: ```text build serve parser → get_kwargs(VllmConfig) → default_factory() → CompilationConfig.__post_init__() → platform and compiler defaults ``` Nor can we simply replace every nested config with a dictionary: [the parser contract][compilation-test] includes returning a real `CompilationConfig` for both omitted and explicit inputs. Explicit JSON values already construct and validate nested configs during parsing. ## Proposed boundary ```mermaid flowchart TD CLI["Command selection"] --> P["Build selected parser"] C["Existing config
field metadata"] --> P B["Platform metadata
and extension hooks"] --> P P --> H["Help:
no default construction"] P --> V["Convert supplied values"] V --> D["Convert omitted defaults"] D --> N["Return typed Namespace"] N --> E["EngineArgs resolves
model / device settings"] E --> R["Runtime config / engine"] ``` **Command and package loading.** Command modules remain the registry, with cheap names, descriptions and dispatch methods. Only the selected command builds its full parser. Separately, `import vllm` should stop importing Torch as a side effect. Environment settings that must precede Torch stay early; version-specific patches must still run before vLLM uses their targets. This needs both import orders checked. **Field lookup.** Make `get_kwargs()` a lazy mapping over the existing fields. Looking up a flag computes that field's parser metadata; an unused field does no factory work. Cache metadata and keep caller mutations isolated, as today's deep copy does. This avoids a second, hand-maintained list of exposed fields. **Nested config defaults.** For a field whose factory is exactly its config class, use `default="{}"` with the existing JSON converter. Argparse already converts string defaults during parsing. Help can describe `{}` as “use the config defaults,” while a successful parse still returns the real config object. Explicit values use the same converter as today. [Argparse's default conversion][argparse-default]. A focused check with the current `CompilationConfig` converter supports this: constructing the small parser and printing help made zero calls to its post-init; omitted input made one and returned a config equal to today's default. Explicit empty/non-default JSON, invalid input, repeated parses and `parse_known_args` behaved as expected. Config was imported normally before this check; it establishes the conversion mechanism, not Torch-free help. This changes the displayed default in help and generated argument docs from an initialized config dump to `{}`, and moves default construction into parsing. Repeated parses also receive fresh config objects. Literal defaults and deliberate `None` overrides stay intact. Apply this only where empty JSON is equivalent to the declared constructor; it uses Pydantic's JSON path, and a custom factory must not silently become `{}`. Nested subparsers and direct `parser.get_default()` callers still need qualification. No new deferred-value framework is needed for the demonstrated case. The ordering change needs an explicit check: today these factories run before the platform's parser hook; under this proposal they run after it. An extension that changes config state could therefore affect the result. Factory failures also move into argparse's error handling. Those cases need a comparison before changing a field, even if its successful default value matches. `CompilationConfig()` still leaves settings such as compilation mode to later engine setup; parsing does not resolve every runtime default. **Platform and plugin behavior.** Preserve host-specific choices and pre-parse extension hooks. I would have platform selection expose the chosen built-in backend's identifier and device type without loading its implementation class. Share those small declarations with the runtime platform, so the parser does not maintain a second set of choices. Use the same selection rules for both, including explicit CPU selection and out-of-tree platform precedence. Do not broaden accepted device values merely to avoid detecting the platform. Enabled extensions retain their registration path and may import runtime libraries. A later no-argument platform hook cannot replace a hook that adds flags to a parser. Built-in side effects also need care: ROCm's hook sets an environment variable. Its setup must remain before the operations that depend on it. [Platform selection][platform-selection], [hook contract][platform-hook], [ROCm setup][rocm-hook]. **Pydantic and runtime types.** Config already uses Pydantic dataclasses. The shared `@config` decorator builds a schema, and its utility module itself imports Torch for value normalization. `ModelConfig.dtype` and `LoRAConfig.lora_dtype` accept Torch dtype objects as well as specific strings; `DeviceConfig.device` skips Pydantic validation but performs runtime normalization in post-init. [Decorator and utilities][config-utils], [model dtype][model-dtype], [LoRA dtype][lora-dtype], [device config][device]. Those contracts must survive making the declarations cheap to inspect. A focused proof should describe the fields with Torch blocked, then check the existing accepted/rejected inputs and normalization under normal runtime imports. Replacing an annotation with `Any` does not establish that. Python callers constructing config directly should keep their current behavior. The exact type adapter remains an implementation question, rather than a reason to add a parallel schema. The strict import target is ordinary built-in `--help`, `--version` and `serve --help=all`, with extensions disabled and without explicit nested config values. A supplied JSON config can invoke runtime validation before a later help flag; a third-party extension can load its backend. Neither should be silently bypassed to satisfy an import test. ## Prior work and alternatives [#41518](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41518) establishes that the import cleanup can make full help substantially cheaper: a matched rerun on its August base reduced the median from **3.51 s to 0.28 s**, with identical help output. It moves imports to use sites, builds a selected parser, reads built-in device types through a small lookup, and limits aggregate default evaluation to named fields. Its parser platform hook runs only when an out-of-tree platform plugin is present; general plugin loading remains. Those mechanisms need a current-main compatibility audit. Where its code is reused, Netanel will remain a co-author. The Pydantic-settings work in [#42136](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42136) concerns environment-variable definitions and validation. It is useful precedent for deriving behavior from declarations, but does not by itself remove config imports or runtime factories from this parser. | Alternative | Why I would not use it here | | --- | --- | | Generate CLI definitions or help | Introduces an artifact that must track config; it does not resolve runtime defaults or plugin contracts. | | Separate `config_specs` / inherited base | Our prototype added machinery while the serve parser still imported the config package. Moving fields also lost the existing field-docstring check. | | Add CLI metadata to existing fields | Could reduce registration boilerplate later. It does not remove imports, constructors or platform hooks by itself. | ## Implementation and review I would land this in small pieces after agreement on the boundary: selected-command loading, package initialization, then config import chains and default handling. The local command-loading prototype is evidence for the first piece; it does not implement the full design. A fresh-process import check can tighten with each change. It should track the heavy package families still permitted for each command, rather than brittle exact module counts. Compare help, parsed values, errors and effective runtime config against the same base. Any deliberate help-default change should have an explicit before/after example. Keep coverage for enabled plugins and nested config inputs alongside the import check. Linux serving checks must cover both model runners, registration, Torch patches and config hashes. The main tradeoff for review is the runtime-default boundary: **show the declared config input in help, then construct its value through the existing converter during parsing, preserving typed arguments and pre-parse extensions.** I recommend that over calculating a host-specific config dump just to print help. If that boundary is acceptable, the first implementation can stay small without committing us to a generator or a second set of config definitions.
Measurements, current-source probes and limits Historical timings used macOS arm64, Python 3.12.13, Torch 2.11, fresh processes, warm files and `VLLM_PLUGINS=''`. They used a shared environment with source overlays, not rebuilt wheels. Times include Python startup. | Source | Three runs (seconds) | Median | | --- | --- | --- | | Main `711fc55c` | 3.3338, 3.3554, 3.3862 | 3.3554 s | | #41518 base `7ca49fbe` | 3.4444, 3.5068, 3.7607 | 3.5068 s | | #41518 head `b8bc7028` | 0.2816, 0.2805, 0.2788 | 0.2805 s | The matched historical pair had one excluded warm-up per arm. All six measured runs exited 0 and produced identical 124,918-byte help, SHA256 `cb276189432cbc3759ab104c9b664808579a25667b8bd7120568999722df5b9e`. The `711fc55c` row is a separate baseline, not that pair's control. A separate probe on the historical head passed full help with Torch, Transformers, FastAPI and OpenAI blocked. This does not establish runtime or extension compatibility. On September 24, eleven CPU-only subprocess probes used clean main `7a940669` and its local command-loading child `8e6e6789`. These instrumented runs observed calls, not performance. Loaded vLLM Python paths and hashes were recorded; the shared generated version module was tracked separately. Top-level, serve and benchmark help on main all loaded the four heavy package families and constructed config defaults. A temporary synthetic platform plugin added an integer flag; a general plugin logged registration. The comparison preserved version/help stdout, accepted the custom integer before serve help, and rejected an invalid value with exit 2. Parser-hook calls changed as follows: | Invocation | Main | Command-loading prototype | | --- | --- | --- | | `--version` | serve, launch-render, run-batch | none | | serve help with custom flag | serve, launch-render, run-batch | serve | | `bench latency --help` | serve, launch-render, throughput, run-batch | throughput | Both versions still discovered the platform. General-plugin registration still ran for selected serve and benchmark help. Benchmark help still built the throughput parser within the selected benchmark tree. This qualifies one synthetic extension and top-level command selection; it does not prove every extension works or that all unselected nested parsers are avoided. Raw stderr was not byte-identical: imports emitted process/address-specific macOS native-library warnings. The CLI error line matched. The separate string-default fixture used the existing `CompilationConfig` converter after normal imports. Omitted input and explicit `{}` each constructed one equal config; a non-default input preserved its backend and capture sizes; invalid input exited 2. Help constructed none. Repeated parses returned equal but distinct objects with distinct mutable option dictionaries. `parse_known_args` also returned a typed config. This is a proof for one field, not a change to the full parser. No current-main full-help speedup is claimed. Integration of the default change and Torch-free type validation remain unimplemented. CUDA/ROCm behavior, installed Linux behavior and serving need qualification for those changes. These measurements do not establish a serving-startup improvement.

title: [RFC]: KVPP (KV pipeline parallel, LayerSplit) for vLLM
body:
### Motivation.

This proposal is inspired by **Section 4, “LayerSplit,”** of Z.ai's [*Scaling Pain of Coding Agent Serving: Lessons from Debugging GLM-5 at Scale*](https://z.ai/blog/scaling-pain). LayerSplit introduces layer-wise ownership of KV-cache storage and makes the cache available to the other ranks when a layer runs. This RFC describes how to express that idea in vLLM's KV-cache planning and model-execution lifecycle.

An experimental implementation already exists in [vllm-ascend's KVPP design](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/main/developer_guide/Design_Documents/kvpp/) and [feature guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/main/user_guide/feature_guide/kvpp/).

### Terminology: why “KV-PP”

The existing implementation calls this feature **KVPP**, short for **KV pipeline parallel**. We propose writing the same name as **KV-PP** when explaining the parallelism axis. If vLLM's Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) is viewed, at the KV-storage level, as **KV-CP**—partitioning a sequence's KV tokens across ranks—then KV-PP is the complementary **layer-axis** partition: ranks persist different layers' KV caches and obtain a complete layer before using it.

| Conceptual axis | Persistent KV ownership | Access during attention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| KV-CP analogy (DCP) | Different token or context portions of a layer | Distributed attention uses the rank-local context and combines results. |
| KV-PP (this RFC) | Different complete layers | The layer owner makes its cache available to all computing ranks before cache access. |

### Goals

- Increase the logical cache-block capacity when replicated, persistent KV storage is the limiting resource.
- Keep scheduler block IDs, prefix-cache semantics, and request admission based on one complete logical KV-cache specification.
- Allow a device backend to choose layer owners, physical layouts, and a collective transport without teaching the scheduler about those details.
- Define synchronization and connector rules so that a cache read, write, offload, or remote transfer cannot observe an incomplete layer.

### Expected serving benefit and supporting evidence

The primary benefit is **higher throughput when a tiered KV pool serves long, repeatedly reused prefixes that exceed HBM capacity**. KV-PP reduces persistent per-rank KV storage by assigning each layer to an owner, leaving room for more cache blocks and more prefixes in HBM. A pool can then serve more prefix hits from HBM instead of loading them from a slower tier. The [vllm-ascend KVPP PR #16094](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/16094) describes this supporting *follow-up integration benchmark* on Ascend A5 with an AscendStoreConnector/Memcache CPU pool of 32 GB per device, warmed prefix families larger than HBM, and approximately 90% shared prefix:

| Configuration | Input-token throughput, KV-PP off → on | HBM prefix-hit rate, off → on |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| One node, 8 dies | 66,362.5 → 97,318.3 tokens/s (**+46.65%**) | 8.46% → 45.46% |
| Two nodes, 16 dies, PP2 | 86,438.8 → 125,699.3 tokens/s (**+45.42%**) | 0.59% → 53.87% |

PR #16094 itself reports a **5.35×–8.17× increase in logical KV-cache token capacity** across its tested configurations; that capacity creates the opportunity for the observed pooling benefit.

This is consistent with the *scenario and mechanism* in [Z.ai's LayerSplit report, Section 4](https://z.ai/blog/scaling-pain): long-context requests with high cache reuse benefit when layer-wise KV placement relieves device-memory pressure. Z.ai reports **10%–132% throughput gains** for 40K–120K requests at a 90% cache-hit rate. Its workload, model, hardware, and throughput metric differ from the Ascend integration benchmark, so the percentages are independent results rather than a direct comparison.

Without a capacity-constrained KV pool, the extra full-layer broadcasts can outweigh the memory benefit: PR #16094 reports **2.30%–12.77% lower input-token throughput** across its A5 non-pooling tests. This is the counterexample that motivates evaluating KV-PP together with cache residency and transfer metrics, rather than treating capacity growth as an unconditional speedup.

### Proposed Change.

### 1. Separate logical KV planning from physical placement

The model runner continues to report the **complete per-layer `KVCacheSpec`**. vLLM's engine groups those specs, chooses a common block count, and supplies the same logical block numbering to the scheduler and workers. A backend-provided placement plan then maps each layer to an owner rank and describes the worker-local physical cost.

For a first implementation, use a group contained within one data-parallel replica and one pipeline-parallel stage. A group may span TP ranks, or TP × PCP ranks when the backend produces replicated KV in that domain. Replicated, identical KV updates across the group are a prerequisite for retaining updates only on the owner; a backend with TP-sharded KV heads would need a different gather or writeback protocol. Layers local to the PP stage are ordered deterministically and assigned in balanced, contiguous partitions. A layer's main KV, indexer cache, and associated scales form one ownership bundle. Draft-model caches that must remain local are excluded from target-layer partitioning.

For rank `r`, a simple conservative budget is:

```text
bytes_per_logical_block(r) =
    bytes_for_layers_owned_by(r)
  + bytes_for_rank_local_draft_caches(r)
  + 2 × bytes_for_largest_target_layer_bundle

max_blocks(r) = floor(available_KV_bytes(r) / bytes_per_logical_block(r))
```

The engine still selects a block count that every worker can allocate. The placement plan must use the same group-relative rank and layout in both memory budgeting and allocation. The two scratch buffers permit one layer to be consumed while the next is prefetched. Backends may later provide a different buffer policy, but any such policy must be included in the budget.

### 2. Allocate owner storage and reusable receive buffers

On each rank, allocate persistent storage only for its owned target layers and any independent local caches. Allocate two reusable scratch buffers sized for the largest target-layer bundle. Every component of one bundle must have a stable, agreed byte layout so one collective can transfer it. Attention layers still receive normal cache tensor views; they need not know whether the view points to persistent storage or a scratch buffer.

The physical allocator must consume the **final** `KVCacheConfig.num_blocks` returned by the engine. A backend that cannot represent a cache spec, aliasing relationship, or physical layout must reject KV-PP during configuration or planning rather than allocate an incomplete cache.

### 3. Prefetch one layer ahead during model execution

For a forward pass with previously computed KV, start the first layer's prefetch before its attention work. The owner broadcasts the complete historical bundle to the other ranks on a transfer stream. After Q/KV projections, but before the first cache read or write, the attention backend waits for transfer completion and starts prefetching the next layer. The owner retains the updated cache after the layer executes. A forward pass with no historical KV does not need a historical-cache broadcast.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Scheduler: logical block IDs] --> R[Model runner: prepare input]
    R --> P[KV-PP: prefetch layer i from owner]
    P --> C[Layer i projections]
    C --> W[Wait before first KV access]
    W --> A[Layer i attention and cache update]
    W --> N[Prefetch layer i + 1]
    A --> O[Owner retains updated layer i cache]
    N --> X[Next layer]
    O --> X
```

The readiness event must cover preceding cache writes, and the completion event must cover device-side reads of the owner's source and writes to receivers. Every rank in a group must make the same broadcast decision and issue collectives in the same layer order. With PCP, that decision must use the global scheduled batch rather than a rank-local token segment.

The initial scope is **prefill nodes** in disaggregated serving, where layer prefetch can be scheduled ahead of cache-consuming attention and has a meaningful opportunity to overlap communication with computation. Decode has much less computation per token, so simple one-layer-ahead prefetch is unlikely to hide the broadcast reliably. Decode-side KV-PP requires finer control over transfer timing and cache use in the actual attention backend and operators; it will be a separate follow-up.

### 4. Make external KV transfer ownership-aware

KV connectors should register only persistent owner buffers and independent local caches; scratch buffers are temporary and must never be advertised as durable KV. A producer with layer-sharded storage must publish per-layer ownership so a consumer can select a rank that actually holds each layer. A pool lookup must account for every required owner shard before declaring a prefix complete. Connector load completion must precede the attention-side KV-PP wait and cache access.

The first version should define explicit compatibility gates for each connector and parallelism combination. A connector should opt in only after its layer-ownership, completeness, and load-before-use contracts have been verified. This keeps the core vLLM contract independent of any particular KV pool or transfer implementation.

### Trade-offs and alternatives

KV-PP exchanges persistent cache memory for full-layer broadcast traffic. The first implementation broadcasts all allocated blocks in a layer, including inactive blocks; its communication volume therefore grows with provisioned capacity. Prefetch can overlap some of that cost with projections and attention, but the overlap is workload- and backend-dependent. Per-request or per-active-block transfer could reduce bytes but requires a more complex ownership, packing, and synchronization protocol. Replicating all layers avoids the collective but retains the memory bottleneck. DCP shards the context axis and changes attention execution, so it addresses a different dimension and is not an interchangeable implementation of layer ownership.


### Feedback Period.

~2 weeks

### CC List.

@ZJY0516 @NickLucche @LucasWilkinson @GirasoleY @ivanium 

### Any Other Things.

### Co-Author
@recky-c

- Reference implementation: [vllm-ascend KVPP documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/main/user_guide/feature_guide/kvpp/).
- Original inspiration and attribution: [Z.ai, Section 4 “LayerSplit”](https://z.ai/blog/scaling-pain).
