Unconstrained requests on the same server: 0 errors. The `guidance` backend on the same server configuration: 39,532 requests, 0 errors. The default `xgrammar`: 0 errors on 2026-09-18. ### Cause Reproducible without a GPU by driving vLLM's own `OutlinesGrammar` the way the engine does (`repro_outlines_backend_rejects_eos.py`, attached): ``` accept_tokens('yes') : True guide.is_finished(): True bitmask now allows : [151645] (eos allowed: True ) accept_tokens([eos]) : False <-- the engine reads False as 'grammar rejected tokens' and answers 500 ``` After the regex is matched, `outlines_core`'s `Guide` is finished; `fill_bitmask` then allows exactly one token, EOS, so the sampler emits EOS; and `OutlinesGrammar.accept_tokens([eos])` calls `Guide.accepts_tokens([eos])`, which returns False because the guide refuses any token once finished. `vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_outlines.py` already carries a workaround for half of this — `is_terminated()` delays the finished flag by one step "so EOS can still be emitted" — but `accept_tokens` gets no such tolerance, and the scheduler treats its False as a rejection (`scheduler.py:1841`). A fix that matches the existing workaround: in `OutlinesGrammar.accept_tokens`, when the guide is already finished and the tokens are exactly `[eos]`, return True without advancing (the mask allowed nothing else, so nothing else can arrive). **_A related issue in `json_object`_** `response_format: {"type":"json_object"}` under the outlines backend is accepted by the server and then fails inside the engine at `compile_grammar`,`ValueError: Invalid request type for Outlines backend (StructuredOutputOptions.JSON_OBJECT)`, which the client sees as a 500 (5,518 of 5,518 such requests in the same run). The backend does not support that request type; the request should be refused with a 400 at validation (`validate_structured_output_request_outlines`), not fail after admission. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Performance][ROCm] V2 runner PP side streams make gfx1201 (RDNA4) forward ~2× slower; main-stream option fixes it
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

## Summary

On AMD gfx1201 (Radeon AI PRO R9700), a stream of small kernels picks up about 17 µs per dispatch when two or more other HIP streams hold pending waits on it (default hardware-queue limit, graph mode). The driver/runtime side, with a framework-free HIP reproducer, is reported at https://github.com/ROCm/legacy-rocm-build/issues/6685.

The V2 GPU model runner creates exactly that situation on the last pipeline-parallel stage:

- `PPHandler.broadcast()` (and the draft-token broadcast) in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py` runs `broadcast_stream.wait_stream(main_stream)` and then enqueues the sends on `broadcast_stream`.
- The async output path copies results device-to-host on its own copy stream, which also waits on the main stream.

So while the next step's graph runs, two side queues are waiting on the main stream. On gfx1201 that roughly doubles the time of the dispatch-heavy decode forward. The gfx1030 (V620) control was unaffected; NVIDIA was not tested.

## Measurements

The setup was PP=3 and TP=1 with ranks on V620, V620 and R9700 (last rank). It used an MoE hybrid model with MTP2 speculative decoding, FULL HIP graphs and ROCm 7.14.

| Configuration | R9700 forward (15 layers), median | Pipeline step period | Decode throughput |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Side streams (default) | ~16.9–17.0 ms | ~56–58 ms | ~33 tok/s |
| Last-rank sends and output copy on the main stream | 7.18–7.23 ms | 41.6–42.2 ms | 45.3–46.6 tok/s |

Across 803 measured R9700 forward intervals with the change, every one was below 10 ms. In a separate serving measurement, median decode rose from 31.0 to 46.5 tok/s. The model, weights, placement, graph mode and receiving ranks were unchanged. We have not isolated the individual contribution of each of the two streams, since both were moved together.

### Why not just `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=2`?

In the ROCm microbenchmark, `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=1` or `2` removed the tiny-kernel penalty without code changes. In serving, it also brought the R9700 forward down to ~7.2 ms with the original side streams (B), but it **did not match the main-stream option end to end**:

| Arm | Last-rank main stream | `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES` | R9700 forward median / p90 | Step period median | Three xhigh decode rates | 16K TTFT |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| A | On | Unset | 7.216 / 7.683 ms | 41.744 ms | 48.2 / 48.9 / 42.2 tok/s | 9.900 s |
| B | Off | 2 | 7.220 / 7.656 ms | 52.755 ms | 35.9 / 35.8 / 34.3 tok/s | 9.915 s |
| C | On | 2 | 7.261 / 7.729 ms | 52.239 ms | 35.9 / 36.2 / 37.2 tok/s | 9.954 s |

The V620 rank forwards rose from ~10.9 ms in A to ~12.9–13.1 ms in B. The queue cap appears to serialize communication with compute on every GPU, although we have not isolated the exact source of the added time. So the queue limit is a useful diagnostic but not a serving fix.

On output: temperature-0 generations are not run-to-run identical on this stack even with the same configuration (a restarted A1/A2 control diverged on 2 of 3 prompts). So token-level A/B differences between the settings do not indicate an effect on output quality.

## Proposed change

Add an opt-in setting (an environment variable or a `ParallelConfig` field) that makes the last PP rank enqueue its token and draft broadcasts, and the async output copy, on the current (main) stream instead of dedicated side streams. Then either:

- leave it off by default and document it for gfx12 users, or
- turn it on automatically when `current_platform.is_rocm()` and the device is gfx12, until the ROCm issue is resolved.

The cost is that those small sends and copies no longer overlap with the next step's launch on the main stream. On gfx1201 that is far cheaper than the dispatch penalty. We have a local patch and can open a PR if the maintainers prefer one of these two options.

The same mechanism may be relevant to the unexplained bimodal single-GPU R9700 decode reported in ROCm/ROCm#6347, since the async output copy stream also waits on the main stream without PP. We have not tested that.

### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

_No response_

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

`collect_env.py` was not run; the relevant details are below.

- vLLM: V2 GPU model runner from a vLLM fork at [`1bdbbef`](https://github.com/leapdragon/vllm-rdna2-qwen/commit/1bdbbef4bf1ae67abaad0a05c6225bc519f91694), plus a local overlay. Current vLLM main still calls `broadcast_stream.wait_stream(main_stream)` in [`PPHandler.broadcast`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py) (checked 2026-09-24).
- PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm7.14.0, ROCm 7.14 (HIP 7.14.60850), Ubuntu 24.04.4, Linux 6.8, amdgpu DKMS 6.19.14; R9700 MES firmware 0x91.
- GPUs: 2× Radeon Pro V620 (gfx1030) and 1× Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201); PP=3, TP=1.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Description In vLLM 0.29.0's V1 model runner, a completed request can leave its `prompt_embeds` tensor referenced by `InputBatch.req_prompt_embeds`. After all requests have been removed and the persistent batch is empty, the dictionary still contains one tensor for every slot that previously handled a prompt-embedding request. Reusing those slots with ordinary token-ID requests does not release or overwrite the old tensors. They remain alive until another prompt-embedding request overwrites the same slot, the dictionary is cleared, or the worker exits. The retention is bounded by persistent-batch capacity, but a worker can keep the peak prompt-embedding footprint of a previous burst even after ordinary text requests replace that workload. The reproducer retains 256 MiB across eight reused slots and releases it only when the stale dictionary is cleared. At a `max_num_seqs` of 256, the same `(4096, 4096)` BF16 shape can retain up to 8 GiB of host memory. This can increase host-memory pressure, swapping, allocation failures, or container eviction risk. Stale entries can also cause unnecessary prompt-embedding staging work for replacement requests. ## Reproduction Use the script [repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32476544/repro_slot_retention.py), with vLLM 0.29.0 installed, run: ```bash python repro.py 2>&1 | tee reproducer.log ``` The script reproduces a prompt-embedding burst followed by ordinary text traffic: 1. fills eight slots with `(4096, 4096)` BF16 prompt-embedding tensors, totaling 256 MiB; 2. completes all eight requests and forces garbage collection; 3. reuses every slot with an unrelated token-ID request; 4. verifies that every old tensor is still attached to the reused slot; and 5. clears only `req_prompt_embeds` as a control while the text requests remain active. The script records both weak-reference liveness and process RSS. It calls `malloc_trim()` only after clearing the dictionary so that the RSS control is visible; the weak references establish tensor lifetime independently of the allocator. ## Actual result ```text After the embedding requests finish: active request IDs: [] req_prompt_embeds keys: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] live old tensors: 8 live old tensor bytes: 268435456 process RSS bytes: 1166053376 After text requests reuse the same slots: active request IDs: [text-request-0, ..., text-request-7] req_prompt_embeds keys: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] live old tensors: 8 live old tensor bytes: 268435456 stale entries still reference the old tensors: true process RSS bytes: 1166053376 After clearing only req_prompt_embeds: active request IDs: [text-request-0, ..., text-request-7] req_prompt_embeds keys: [] live old tensors: 0 live old tensor bytes: 0 process RSS bytes: 896708608 RSS drop bytes: 269344768 ``` The weak-reference control shows that the stale dictionary entries are the remaining owners of the tensors. The text requests remain active when the old tensors are released, so the tensors are not needed by the replacement requests. The complete output is in [reproducer_slot_retention.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32476576/reproducer_slot_retention.log). ## Expected result Once a request is removed, its slot must no longer own the request's prompt-embedding tensor. With an empty batch, `req_prompt_embeds` should be empty. Reusing the slots with token-ID requests should not keep any tensor from the completed requests alive. ## Root cause [`InputBatch.add_request()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.29.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py#L350-L386) stores the tensor by slot index: ```python if request.prompt_embeds is not None: self.req_prompt_embeds[req_index] = request.prompt_embeds ``` [`InputBatch.remove_request()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.29.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py#L528-L582) clears the other request-scoped state but never removes this entry. The empty-batch branch of [`condense()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.29.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py#L706-L727) also leaves the dictionary unchanged. The missing cleanup can be performed as soon as the request index is known: ```python self.req_prompt_embeds.pop(req_index, None) ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/torchinductor_lazychaser
```


### How would you like to use vllm

Serious performance degradation 0.26 vs 0.27. My config:

```yaml

title: [RFC]: The dynamic-SD K decision is a batch-keyed array index — agreeing on its shape before more signals arrive
body:
### Motivation.

On current `main` (`504bb8b0c3`) the dynamic-SD K decision is one array index:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:1321-1324
if self.dynamic_sd_lookup is not None and len(num_scheduled_tokens) > 0:
    num_spec_tokens_to_schedule = self.dynamic_sd_lookup[
        len(num_scheduled_tokens)
    ]
```

The key is batch size, and that choice is fixed in four places, not one:

- `validate_and_normalize_dynamic_sd_schedule` unpacks entries as
  `(range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens)` (`dynamic/utils.py:37`)
- `build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup` returns `list[int]`, a dense
  `batch_size -> K` table (`dynamic/utils.py:77-81`)
- the scheduler indexes it by `len(num_scheduled_tokens)` (`sched/scheduler.py:1322`)
- since #50488, two capture-planning sites read the same dense table
  (`worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:219`, `config/vllm.py:2067`)

The decision site is not short of information — `schedule()` has the request set
in hand, so per-request `num_computed_tokens`, acceptance history and queue
depth are all in scope. They are simply not read. Whatever a proposal wants K to
depend on, it currently has to widen that tuple everywhere, or bypass the
schedule entirely.

**Six different signals are being proposed for this one decision right now.**
Batch size is what ships. Beyond it:

| signal | where |
|---|---|
| context length | #48944 (mine), widening the tuple to `(bs, ctx) -> K` |
| token entropy | #54082, gating K between 0 and K at runtime |
| marginal gain | LibraSpec, [2608.08721](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08721) |
| expert activation cost | EcoSpec, [2607.12696](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12696) |
| step-wise efficiency (entropy-controlled length) | SparseSpec-L, [2607.27735](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27735) |
| learned verification payoff | Hybrid Verified Decoding, [2606.01019](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01019) |

Two of those papers converge on the same criterion. SparseSpec-L states it
directly: *"extending the speculation horizon can reduce rather than improve
speedup when the marginal acceptance probability falls below the relative
drafting cost."*

I am not asking for any of them to be adopted. I am asking whether the K
decision should keep being a batch-keyed array index, given that the next six
proposals all need it not to be.

> **Update, 2026-09-07 — prior art I should have cited, and a seventh signal.**
>
> **#38038** (`Dynamic SD scheduler decides`, draft, opened 2026-03-24) already
> answers the question this RFC asks, and I did not find it before posting. It
> adds `vllm/v1/spec_decode/dynamic/manager.py` —
> `DynamicSpeculativeDecodingManager`, which picks K by maximizing
> `goodput = acceptance_length / ITL` over a profiled `batch_stats[bs][K] -> ITL`
> table, refreshes its per-position acceptance rates from live
> `SpecDecodingStats` after a warmup period, and interpolates between measured
> batch sizes and K values. It is a policy object, not an array index, and it is
> the most developed K controller in the tree.
>
> It is also keyed on batch size alone: `step(batch_size) -> int`, and the
> companion `generate_config.py` sweeps `(batch_size, K)` on a fixed dataset to
> produce `{batch_size: {num_drafts: median_itl_ms}}`. ITL is context-dependent,
> so in that design context is a constant of the profiling run rather than an
> input to the policy.
>
> That is the sharpest form of what this RFC is asking about, and it points the
> question at the maintainers more than at me: the one component here that was
> built as a policy rather than a table still cannot express a context-dependent
> K, and it has been dormant since 2026-05-07. Whether that is the intended
> destination for this decision is exactly what I do not know.
>
> Separately, a seventh signal has since been proposed and implemented:
> **#54801** adds `num_speculative_tokens_per_seq_len` as a second table
> consulted only when the batch-size table is unset, prompted by **#54691**,
> which reports speculation becoming a net loss at 185k context and states that
> no per-sequence-length hook exists today. I have commented there rather than
> restate it here. That is two new entries to the table above in the six days
> since this was opened, which is the part I would ask maintainers to weigh.

### Evidence I can offer, with its limits.

I ran the (batch, ctx) case, so the numbers below are about that one signal.
Full provenance, including what I have withdrawn, is in a
[ledger](https://github.com/seongyun1104/depthchart/blob/931ff25/EVIDENCE_LEDGER.md);
the per-cell working is in a
[companion note](https://github.com/seongyun1104/depthchart/blob/931ff25/POLICY_INTERFACE.md).

**1. The win localises to a single cell.** Position-balanced 2 trials, cache
wiped per launch, cold-start burn, 3 warm-up discarded + 3 measured per cell,
c=256, per-arm stdev at most 1.72 %, Gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-FP8 with its assistant
drafter on one H100 NVL. A batch-only schedule `[[1,64,3],[65,128,1],[129,512,0]]`
against a (bs, ctx) schedule that differs from it in exactly one cell — at
bs ≥ 129 and ctx ≥ 769, K=3 instead of K=0:

| ctx | batch-only | (bs, ctx) | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|:-:|
| 400 | 1875.6 | 1890.7 | 1.01× |
| 900 | 1453.5 | 1874.6 | 1.29× |
| 1900 | 1416.6 | 1848.2 | 1.30× |
| 4000 | 1232.8 | 1680.4 | 1.36× |

The ctx=400 tie is the design working: there both schedules select K=0. The
mechanism is narrow and worth stating plainly — **at high batch a batch-only
schedule has to turn speculation off, and context is what tells you when to turn
it back on.**

The distinct-K set is `{0, 1, 3}` for both schedules, so this costs no extra
CUDA graphs; graphs are keyed on K, and the K values are the same ones.

**2. A cost model over the same interface gets that cell wrong.** I also have a
producer that derives the schedule from a stated cost model rather than typing
it — `K* = argmax_K E_accept(K) / (F(ctx) + K·M(bs))`, the same marginal-utility
shape LibraSpec and SparseSpec-L arrive at. Run with the coefficients it ships,
sweeping only the acceptance prior across 0.35–0.75 (the campaign observed
44–47 % in the K=3 tier), it selects **K=0 at the high-batch tier at every
context**. It reproduces the batch-only schedule and would not have found the
cell worth 29–36 %.

That gap closes under recalibration — the per-context coefficient has to be
roughly an order of magnitude larger relative to the per-batch one — not under a
change of functional form. I am reporting it because it is the honest state of
that producer: a stated model, uncalibrated, currently disagreeing with my own
measurement.

**3. What I have not established.** One model pair, one hardware configuration,
one concurrency, four context points, one differing cell. I have not calibrated
the cost model on hardware. I have not attributed the DSD baseline tax to its
terms — the 2×2 design for that is written and unrun. And the sharpness of the K
optimum at low batch did not clear its own pre-registered bar (#48627, and see
the ledger); the result above is at c=256, which is a different regime.

### Proposed Change.

**None yet — this asks for a decision, not a design.** I have a stake here
(#48944 is the ctx-axis version) and I would rather the shape be agreed before
more signals arrive than argue for mine.

The question is where the K decision should live:

1. **Keep it batch-keyed** and let each new signal negotiate its own widening.
   Predictable, and the dense array stays trivially cheap. #50488 has just made
   this the assumption in two more places, so this is the status quo by default
   rather than by decision.
2. **Let the schedule declare its own key set**, so `(bs, ctx)` and any later
   key are the same kind of object to the consumers. This is what #48944 does
   for one extra key; generalising it is a small change to the validator, the
   lookup and the three read sites.
3. **Separate the decision from the schedule**, so that a table, a cost model,
   or a runtime controller are interchangeable producers of K. Two producers
   already exist behind one schedule in my branch, which is the minimum evidence
   for this being more than speculative generality — but two is also the
   minimum, and I would not argue for it on that basis alone.

What I think matters more than which option: **nothing in the engine currently
measures the quantity these policies need.** Acceptance is exported in aggregate,
but per-`(batch bucket, ctx bucket, K)` draft and verify latency, first-rejection
position, committed tokens per verification, and K-keyed graph hit/miss are not.
My cost model missed the cell above because its coefficients were guesses; there
is no way to stop them being guesses from inside vLLM today. If only one thing
comes out of this thread, that telemetry is the one I would pick, and it is
independent of which option above wins.

I have opened #54748 for the smallest piece of it, so this is not a request for
someone else to do the work: steps the schedule sends to K=0 build no
`SpecDecodingStats` at all, so a schedule that has correctly stopped speculating
under load is indistinguishable from speculative decoding not running. That PR
adds a step counter keyed on the selected K and is deliberately independent of
everything proposed here.

### Feedback Period.

No deadline. I will not open a PR against any of the three options without
agreement here first.

### Any Other Things.

Related: RFC #48627 (the ctx axis specifically, with its evidence section
corrected on 2026-09-01), PR #48944, #54082, #49986, #49548, #48494.

Prior art on the ctx dependence itself: MagicDec
([blog](https://infini-ai-lab.github.io/MagicDec-part1/), paper
[2408.11049](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11049)) proposes choosing speculation
amount as a function of sequence length; TurboSpec/SmartSpec
([2406.14066](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14066)) is the batch-adaptive
predecessor of the schedule API this RFC is about.



> **Update, 2026-09-13 — this RFC left out the controller that actually shipped, and with it in view the question gets sharper.**
>
> My 2026-09-07 update said of #38038 that *"whether that is the intended destination for
> this decision is exactly what I do not know."* It is answerable, and I should have
> answered it here rather than leaving it open: the destination was **#47808**
> (`[Spec Decode] DSpark confidence-scheduled verification`, merged 2026-08-12), which
> added `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/adaptive_verification.py`. RFC #48627 cites it;
> this RFC does not, which makes the Motivation section above read as though the dense
> `batch_size -> K` array were the only controller in the tree. It is not, and the
> omission is mine.
>
> **#38038 and #47808 are the same author's two answers to this RFC's question.** Both are
> @LucasWilkinson's. Both choose a speculation budget by maximizing goodput. Both price
> context once, before serving, and then hold it fixed.
>
> | | #38038 (open, draft, dormant since 2026-05-07) | #47808 (merged 2026-08-12) |
> |---|---|---|
> | objective | `acceptance_length / ITL` | estimated accepted tokens / cost |
> | cost table keyed on | `batch_stats[bs][K] -> ITL` | `num_reqs`, `num_target_tokens` |
> | context | constant of the profiling run | constant of the profiling run |
>
> For #47808 that is visible in three places. The budget is a goodput argmax
> (`adaptive_verification.py:342`):
>
> ```python
> draft_budget = int(np.argmax(num_tokens_to_estimated_accepted_tokens / costs))
> ```
>
> `costs` is assembled from two profiled curves, neither of which carries a context axis —
> `set_initial_cost_curves` builds `draft_curve` keyed on `s.num_reqs` and `verify_curve`
> keyed on `s.num_target_tokens`:
>
> ```python
>         costs = (
>             draft_cost_ms[len(req_ids)]
>             + verify_cost_ms[
>                 num_non_draft_tokens_total : num_non_draft_tokens_total
>                 + max_draft_budget
>                 + 1
>             ]
>         )
> ```
>
> And context enters exactly once, in `batches_to_profile`, held fixed across every sample:
>
> ```python
>                 yield {
>                     "num_tokens": num_tokens,
>                     "context_len": envs.VLLM_ADAPTIVE_VERIFICATION_PROFILE_CONTEXT_LEN,
>                 }
> ```
>
> That env var defaults to 8192. Its comment in `envs.py` states the consequence directly:
> *"Raise it for long-context deployments, where step cost is dominated by attention over
> a much larger KV cache than the default assumes."* The feature documentation says the
> same thing to operators: *"Deployments serving much longer contexts may want to raise it
> so the profiled step reads a more realistic amount of cache."*
>
> So context is not absent from the shipped controller. It is a **deployment-wide scalar
> set before serving**, not an input the policy reads per step — which is the distinction
> this RFC exists to ask about, and I had been asking it against the weaker example.
>
> To be precise about scope, since it would be easy to overstate: adaptive verification
> does not choose K. Drafting still happens at the scheduled length; it chooses how much
> of the already-drafted block to verify, scoring every (request, position) slot by
> survival probability and admitting the best until the budget is spent. So the array
> index above is still the K decision. But "should a table, a cost model, or a runtime
> controller produce the budget" is not an open question in the way I framed it — a cost
> model shipped in August, and 41 open PRs reference it today.
>
> **The question I would actually ask, now:** the person who owns this decision has
> implemented it twice, three months apart, in two subsystems, and both times context was
> priced once at startup rather than read as an input. @LucasWilkinson — is that a
> deliberate boundary?
>
> It is a real question and either answer is useful to me. If it is deliberate, then
> #48944 and #54801 are both arguing against a decision that has already been made twice
> by the person best placed to make it, and the honest thing is for me to say so on my own
> PR. If it is not deliberate, then the natural place for a context term is
> #47808's cost curves rather than the config tuple I have been widening — a smaller and
> better-located change than the one I have been proposing.
>
> I have no measurement on the adaptive-verification path and am not claiming one.
>
> ---
>
> Two smaller corrections while I am here.
>
> **Coordinates in the Motivation section have drifted.** Refreshed against `main`
> (`fa1b3b1922`): the scheduler index is now `sched/scheduler.py:1393-1397` (was
> `:1321-1324`); the capture-planning reads are `worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:246` (was
> `:219`) and `config/vllm.py:2282` (was `:2067`). `dynamic/utils.py:37` and `:77-81` are
> unchanged, and the quoted block itself is unchanged.
>
> **One piece of external evidence has arrived.** In #54691, @hongboshi1234 measured a
> break-even acceptance surface on B300 / TP8 / DCP-8 with Kimi-K3 and a DFlash drafter —
> different vendor, model family and drafter from mine — by forcing every draft to be
> rejected and comparing per-token latency against no speculation. For any achievable
> accept length in (1.91, 3.51), the resulting pays / does-not-pay region cannot be
> produced by a context rule and a batch rule consulted separately: (2k, B=8) pays, so
> neither rule fires there; (32k, B=8) does not pay, so the context rule must fire at 32k;
> but then (32k, B=1) would be switched off, and it pays. My own result has the opposite
> sign — speculation switched back *on* at high batch when context is long — and the same
> non-separable shape. Two measurements is not many, but they are independent, and the
> second was not looking for this. I checked their proposed *mechanism* and it does not
> hold, which I have said in that thread; the surface stands, the explanation for its
> magnitude is open.


> **Update, 2026-09-20 — walking back one phrase, and a constraint that applies to either answer.**
>
> No answer yet on the question above, which is a fair outcome for a question nobody asked
> for. Two things are worth putting in the record regardless of who decides, because both
> narrow the decision rather than argue for a side.
>
> **First, a correction to my own 2026-09-13 update.** I wrote that a context term in
> #47808's cost curves would be *"a smaller and better-located change"* than widening the
> config tuple. I had not checked that, and having checked it, "better-located" holds but
> **"smaller" does not**. `self.cost_tables` is a pair of 1-D `np.ndarray`
> (`adaptive_verification.py:151`), built by `build_cost_tables_from_curves` (`:81-129`),
> which stitches three regimes together: a step function below the cudagraph capture limit
> where execution pads to the next captured size, linear interpolation above it where
> nothing pads, and linear extrapolation past the last profiled point. A context axis means
> reproducing all three per context slice, and the cudagraph discontinuity is a function of
> token count rather than context, so the axes do not separate cleanly. Profiling would
> also multiply: `batches_to_profile` currently yields
> `(capture_sizes + tail_sizes) × _PROFILE_REPLAYS`, with context pinned to one env value.
>
> **Second, the part that matters more, because it is not a preference.** Wherever the
> context term lives, the same question has to be answered, and I had not noticed that it
> is invariant to the choice.
>
> `get_num_tokens` computes one cost vector for the whole batch:
>
> ```python
>         draft_cost_ms, verify_cost_ms = self.cost_tables
>         costs = (
>             draft_cost_ms[len(req_ids)]
>             + verify_cost_ms[num_non_draft_tokens_total : ...]
>         )
> ```
>
> But a batch holds requests at many different context lengths. Indexing a context-keyed
> cost table requires collapsing them to a single number — and that is exactly the question
> benchislett put to me on #48944 on 2026-07-21:
>
> > *"It's not clear to me what is the right way to aggregate sequence length across a
> > batch. I feel like mean or max … makes more sense than median"*
>
> which #48944 currently exposes as `ctx_agg: Literal["median", "mean", "max"]`.
>
> So the aggregation question is **not** an artifact of the schedule-table design I have
> been proposing. It is a property of putting context into a per-batch budget decision at
> all, and it lands on the shipped controller identically. Whoever decides where the
> context term belongs — including deciding that it belongs nowhere — is deciding this too.
>
> I am noting it rather than answering it. My own answer to benchislett did not hold up:
> I retracted the benchmark evidence for the `mean` default on 2026-09-10 on #48944, because
> two of the four scenarios I had cited turned out to be controls. The knob names a real
> decision; the measurement I offered for its default does not survive, and I would not want
> that distinction lost if someone picks this up.
>
> **Third, a correction I owe on the telemetry ask above.** The Proposed Change section
> says *"nothing in the engine currently measures the quantity these policies need"* and
> picks that telemetry as the one thing worth taking from this thread. Half of that is
> wrong, and I should not have written it without looking harder.
>
> #50919 (`[MRV2] Worker-Level Timings`, open since 2026-08-03, +929/-7) exports exactly
> the latencies I said were missing:
>
> ```
> vllm:worker_spec_decode_proposer_time_seconds   labels: phase, num_requests
> vllm:worker_model_execute_time_seconds          labels: phase, num_model_tokens
> vllm:worker_step_time_seconds                   labels: phase, num_model_tokens
> ```
>
> So draft time and verify time are measured. What survives, and is sharper than what I
> originally wrote, is the **keying**. `WorkerTimingStats` carries `iteration_index`,
> `phase`, `num_model_tokens`, `num_requests`, and the prefill/decode token and request
> splits. It carries no KV context length and no selected K, and the `num_*_tokens` fields
> are query tokens for the step rather than cache depth.
>
> Those are the same two keys as the cost curves in #47808: `draft_curve` keyed on
> `s.num_reqs`, `verify_curve` on `s.num_target_tokens`. And #50919's own stated purpose
> is *"establish reliable statistics for introspective profiling-based tuning such as
> adaptive verification"* — so the instrument is being built to tune the policy, and the
> two share a key set that excludes context.
>
> That is the thing I would now put in place of my original ask. A profiling-driven policy
> cannot discover a dependence on an axis its instrumentation does not record. If context
> is deliberately out of scope for this decision, then this is all consistent and I should
> stop. If it is not deliberate, the cheapest place to find out is a context bucket on the
> proposer timing, long before anything needs to change in a schedule or a config tuple.
>
> I am not raising this on #50919 itself. It is a draft, and I have an open PR that
> benchislett holds review authority over, so a request there for the axis I happen to be
> arguing for would read as exactly what it would be.
>
> **Fourth, something merged after I drafted the rest of this, which changes the scope of
> the question rather than my answer to it.**
>
> #52228 (`[Model Runner V2] Acceptance estimation for adaptive verification`) merged on
> 2026-09-14 as `3bb0a03f35`. Two things about it are worth recording here.
>
> It removed the gate confining adaptive verification to DSpark. `SpeculativeConfig` used
> to raise `"Adaptive verification only supported with DSpark"`, and `DSparkSpeculator`
> additionally required a checkpoint with a trained confidence head. The new
> `OnlineAcceptanceEstimator` predicts per-position acceptance from draft logits that any
> drafter already materializes, so the trained head became an optimization rather than a
> precondition. The controller this thread has been asking about is therefore no longer a
> DSpark feature; on main it is the general adaptive-verification path.
>
> And it makes the shape of the decision visible in a way it was not before, because the
> two sides of the ratio in `get_num_tokens` are now keyed differently from each other.
>
> The benefit side is per-slot. `adaptive_verification.py:314, 326-328`:
>
> ```python
>         scores = np.sort(survival_probability[valid])[::-1]
>         ...
>         num_tokens_to_estimated_accepted_tokens = np.concatenate(
>             ([num_sampling_requests], num_sampling_requests + np.cumsum(scores))
>         )
> ```
>
> `survival_probability` is each request's own running product of per-position
> confidences, so the b-th admitted draft slot contributes `scores[b-1]` expected accepted
> tokens and that quantity belongs to an identifiable request.
>
> The cost side is not. Its marginal term is
> `verify_cost_ms[T+b] - verify_cost_ms[T+b-1]`, a function of the batch's total token
> count, identical no matter which request the slot belongs to. So the descending sort is
> the right admission order exactly when every draft slot costs the same to verify, which
> is what a table keyed on `s.num_target_tokens` encodes.
>
> This refines what I wrote above rather than repeating it. I said the batch-to-scalar
> aggregation question is invariant to where the context term lives. That still holds for
> a **batch-keyed** cost table, which is what both #48944 and #47808 have. What #52228
> shows is that the aggregation is forced by the table's keying and not by pricing context
> as such — because the benefit side prices per slot and never needs a batch reduction at
> all. I had been treating the aggregation as intrinsic. It is not; it is a consequence of
> the shape I picked, and of the shape the shipped cost table picked.
>
> One detail I want to state plainly because it removes the most reasonable objection.
> Per-request KV depth is not unavailable at this decision — it is already read there, at `:322-325`, above the cost expression at `:329`:
>
> ```python
>         num_sampling_requests = np.count_nonzero(
>             self.req_states.num_computed_tokens_np[slots] + num_non_draft_tokens
>             >= self.req_states.prefill_len.np[slots]
>         )
> ```
>
> `num_computed_tokens_np[slots]` is gathered for exactly the requests being priced, used
> to count how many have finished prefill, and not consulted again. So "context is not
> modelled in the cost table" is not a statement about what the scheduler can see.
>
> There is also a timing asymmetry now. The acceptance coefficients refit online every
> 100 steps for the life of the process (`acceptance_estimator.py:330`). The cost curves
> are fitted once, during startup capture — `set_initial_cost_curves` has a single caller,
> `model_runner.py:1044` — at one context length taken from
> `VLLM_ADAPTIVE_VERIFICATION_PROFILE_CONTEXT_LEN`, whose own comment in `envs.py` reads:
>
> > Raise it for long-context deployments, where step cost is dominated by attention over
> > a much larger KV cache than the default assumes.
>
> I am quoting that because it states the dependence better than I have been stating it,
> and because it shows the current answer is not that context does not matter — it is that
> context is an operator-set constant. That is a coherent position. It is the position I
> am asking whether anyone intends.
>
> To be careful about what I am not claiming: the acceptance estimator is **not** context-
> blind. Its feature is computed from the drafter's forward pass over the real prefix, and
> the code says so — *"It scores the draft distribution, not the token drawn from it, so
> it is a function of the prefix alone."* Context reaches the benefit side implicitly,
> through the drafter's own confidence. What is pooled is the fit: one global slope, with
> intercepts keyed on draft position only. Whether that pooling holds across context
> regimes is a question I can state but have not measured, and I would rather leave it
> stated than dress it up.
>
> One note on that pooling, since it stopped being only my reading of the code. #57533
> was opened on 2026-09-18 against the estimator, from a different direction: request-
> specific sampling transforms are applied on the target but not on the draft, so
> accept/reject labels from those requests were being folded into worker-wide coefficients
> that then size verification for unrelated later requests. That is not my question and it
> does not answer it — it concerns which observations are admissible, not which regimes a
> single fit is expected to span. I raise it only because it establishes that the fit being
> shared across heterogeneous requests is load-bearing rather than incidental, which
> otherwise I would be asserting on my own.
>
> Absent a decision here I am going to go and measure the boundary rather than keep arguing
> its shape, and I will report what comes back whichever way it falls. This RFC does not
> need a reply for that to happen.

title: [Bug]: Massive output-token throughput regression since v0.24.0 with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8
body: ### Your current environment Docker image `vllm-openai:v0.24.0 - v0.26.0` ### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Summary I'm seeing a major output-token throughput regression starting with vLLM v0.24.0 and still present in v0.25.0 and v0.26.0. With the same model, workload (40 parallel requests / ~1k input), and configuration: - v0.24.0 / v0.25.0 / v0.26.0: output throughput is dramatically lower, generally below ~1k output tokens/s. - v0.23.0: throughput is much higher, around ~5k output tokens/s under the same workload. The attached graph shows the difference between runs using the different vLLM versions. ### v0.23.0 behavior v0.23.0 gives much better throughput, but after running for some time the pod can enter what looks like a deadlocked/stuck state: - Requests remained reported as in-flight indefinitely. - GPU utilization stayed at ~100%, but no useful inference progress was made. - Output-token generation stopped completely. - No new engine statistics were emitted for 10+ hours. - The API server remained responsive and /health continued returning HTTP 200. - New requests routed to that replica consequently hung until the upstream request timeout. - Restarting the pod was required to recover. This looked like the API process remained healthy while the underlying EngineCore/CUDA execution was stuck. We don't have logs from the exact moment the engine stopped progressing, so I can't confirm whether this was a CUDA/MoE issue, scheduler issue, or something else. This is the main reason I tried upgrading, but the newer versions introduce the large throughput regression described above. ### Configuration The parameters are unchanged between tests: ```yaml vllmConfig: enablePrefixCaching: true tensorParallelSize: 1 extraArgs: - --served-model-name - Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 - --trust-remote-code - --load-format - runai_streamer - --tool-call-parser - qwen3_coder - --reasoning-parser - qwen3 - --mm-encoder-tp-mode - data - --max-num-seqs - 256 ```` I also tested v0.26.0 with the old model runner: ```bash VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 ``` but this did not improve the throughput. ### Question Has anything changed between v0.23.0 and v0.24.0 that could explain such a large decoding/output-token throughput regression for this model/workload? Are there any flags, scheduler/model-runner settings, or metrics/profiling options you would recommend trying to narrow down where the regression is coming from? I'm also interested in any suggestions for diagnosing the stuck/"ghost running requests" behavior on v0.23.0, since otherwise that version performs significantly better. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Performance]: GLM-5.3-Flash on H100: auto-selected FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90 is 36-70% slower than FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE
body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>vllm collect-env (abridged)</summary>

```
OS                           : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
PyTorch version              : 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA runtime version         : 13.0.88
GPU                          : 8x NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (single node, TP=8)
Nvidia driver version        : 595.71.05
vLLM Version                 : 0.28.1rc1.dev580+g385dce36b (git sha: 385dce36b)
Docker image                 : vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash @ sha256:819ec9c063412e5730d1b0e82046ba540d1bf991f3c4f661a849aae8a0c52374
[pip3] flashinfer-python==0.6.18
[pip3] torch==2.13.0+cu130
[pip3] triton==3.7.1
```
</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary:** For `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` on H100 the auto-selected sparse-MLA attention backend is `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90` (log: `Using FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90 attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90', 'FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE']`). It is **~36% slower at concurrency 1 and ~70% slower at concurrency 8** than the other candidate, `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE`, measured with `vllm bench serve` on the same server flags. MTP draft acceptance is identical across the two, so the gap is per-step attention cost, not speculative-decoding behaviour. Forcing `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` recovers it.

**How we found it:** we had been serving from an image built on 2026-08-26 from the `glm-release` branch (base `487ecf187`, FlashInfer 0.6.17). That build logs `Using FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE', 'FLASHMLA_SPARSE']`. After moving to the current `vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash` (nightly `385dce36b`, FlashInfer 0.6.18) with identical flags, the backend line changed to `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90` and single-stream throughput dropped by roughly a third. The preference appears to come from #53906 (`031c899d` "[Model] Use FlashInfer for GLM-5.3-Flash NoPE MLA", `e34f7f71` "[Kernel] Use FlashInfer rc10 for NoPE MLA") and is gated on the FlashInfer version, so the 0.6.17 -> 0.6.18 bump flipped the kernel without any flag change.

**Server launch (both runs identical except the one flag):**

```bash
docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v /path/to/hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  -e VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 \
  vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash \
  zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --served-model-name zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":5}' \
  --tool-call-parser glm47 --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser glm45 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-seqs 512
  # "FA3" rows add:  --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE
```

**Benchmark (run inside the same container):**

```bash
vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --base-url http://localhost:8000 \
  --model zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash --served-model-name zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --dataset-name sonnet --dataset-path /vllm-workspace/benchmarks/sonnet.txt \
  --sonnet-input-len 300 --sonnet-output-len 256 --sonnet-prefix-len 100 \
  --num-prompts 20 --num-warmups 2 --max-concurrency {1,8} --ignore-eos --disable-shuffle --temperature 0 --seed 0
# "random" rows: --dataset-name random --random-input-len 300 --random-output-len 256
```

| dataset | max-concurrency | backend | output tok/s | mean TPOT | mean ITL | median E2E (256 tok) | MTP accept len / rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sonnet | 1 | `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` (forced) | **368.8** | 2.28 ms | 10.9 ms | 698 ms | 4.89 / 77.8% |
| sonnet | 1 | `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90` (default) | 237.0 | 3.83 ms | 18.3 ms | 1064 ms | 4.89 / 77.7% |
| sonnet | 8 | `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` (forced) | **754.1** | 5.00 ms | 23.9 ms | 1914 ms | 4.90 / 77.9% |
| sonnet | 8 | `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90` (default) | 229.8 | 17.4 ms | 82.9 ms | 5470 ms | 4.87 / 77.3% |
| random | 1 | `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` (forced) | **249.3** | 3.59 ms | 10.9 ms | 1006 ms | 3.08 / 41.7% |
| random | 1 | `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90` (default) | 162.9 | 5.78 ms | 17.0 ms | 1570 ms | 2.97 / 39.5% |

(sonnet is a best case for MTP on this model, random a worst case; the ratio between backends is the same in both.) Same picture with `--enable-expert-parallel` (recipe TEP strategy) and with the Hopper recipe override `--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune`.

**Expected:** the auto-selected backend should not be materially slower than an available alternative on the same hardware; or the recipe should document `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` for Hopper.

**Related:** forcing `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` on this nightly floods the log with `Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1` from zero-extent descriptors (outputs correct; 0 such messages with the default backend). Filed separately: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56563.

title: [Bug]: FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE emits 'Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1' every step for GLM-5.3-Flash (zero-extent descriptors; output correct)
body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>vllm collect-env (abridged)</summary>

```
OS                           : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
PyTorch version              : 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA runtime version         : 13.0.88
GPU                          : 8x NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (single node, TP=8)
Nvidia driver version        : 595.71.05
vLLM Version                 : 0.28.1rc1.dev580+g385dce36b (git sha: 385dce36b)
Docker image                 : vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash @ sha256:819ec9c063412e5730d1b0e82046ba540d1bf991f3c4f661a849aae8a0c52374
[pip3] flashinfer-python==0.6.18
[pip3] torch==2.13.0+cu130
[pip3] triton==3.7.1
```
</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary:** With `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` and `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` on H100 (TP=8, MTP speculative decoding), every forward step emits ~88 copies of

```
Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1
```

from the FA3 sparse-MLA kernel (`vllm/vllm_flash_attn/_vllm_fa3_C.abi3.so`). The dumped descriptors all have `gmem_address 0` and a zero leading extent, i.e. the kernel is asked to build TMA descriptors for **empty (zero-token) segments**. CUDA rejects them with `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` (1). Generation output is correct (verified on short prompts, a 10k-token needle-count prompt, and greedy essays), so the failure is on an empty segment with nothing to compute — but it is emitted on every step in both prefill and decode, first appears during CUDA-graph capture, and produces roughly 2 GB/hour of container log at light single-user load.

**Count matches layers x ranks:** 854 messages for one 60-token completion (~11 MTP steps) and 283 for a `max_tokens=1` request => ~80-90 per step = 11 sparse-MLA layers x 8 TP ranks. This looks like the same class of bug as the FlashMLA sparse "phantom / zero-query-length chunk" reports (#49922, #51486, #52339; partial fix in #51489), except FA3 prints and continues instead of asserting.

**Descriptor dumps (representative):**

```
format         9            # BFLOAT16
dim            4
gmem_address   0
globalDim      (0,512,1,1,1)
globalStrides  (2,4096,4096,0,0)
boxDim         (64,64,1,1,1)
elementStrides (1,1,1,1,1)
interleave     0
swizzle        3
l2Promotion    2
oobFill        0
Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1
```

Distinct `globalDim` values observed over ~100k occurrences (count, shape):
```
36694  (0,1,1,2177280,1)
18866  (0,1,1,327680,1)
  687  (0,480,1,1,1)
  547  (0,6,1,1,1)
```

**Launch command:**

```bash
docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v /path/to/hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  -e VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 \
  vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash \
  zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --served-model-name zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":5}' \
  --tool-call-parser glm47 --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser glm45 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-seqs 512
```

Relevant startup lines:
```
Using FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE attention backend ...
Fused multi-step draft decode is not supported by attention backend(s) DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER, FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE, KPOOL_TAIL; falling back to rebuilding attention metadata between draft steps.
```

**Reproduce:** start as above, then send any chat completion, e.g.
```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi."}],"max_tokens":1}'
docker logs <container> 2>&1 | grep -c "TMA descriptor"   # grows by ~280 for that single request
```

**Not present with the default backend:** the same nightly launched without `--attention-backend` (auto-selects `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90`) logs 0 of these messages across the same benchmark runs.

**Why we are on this backend anyway:** with `vllm bench serve` the auto-selected `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90` is ~36% slower at concurrency 1 and ~70% slower at concurrency 8 than `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` on this model/hardware (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56564), so FA3 is the attractive option — but it should skip TMA descriptor creation / kernel launch when a segment has zero tokens, or the metadata builder should not hand it empty segments. Beyond the log volume, ~88 failing `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` calls plus stderr prints per step are host-side work on the decode critical path, which matters on CPU-constrained hosts.

**Not reproduced on:** an image built locally 2026-08-26 from the `glm-release` branch (base `487ecf187`, FlashInfer 0.6.17), which auto-selected `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` and, as far as we observed, did not emit these messages (not exhaustively checked).

title: [Bug][DSA] Complete sparse top-k output after DeepSelect detects a NaN
body:
## Summary

[vLLM #58215](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58215) correctly bounds DeepSelect's NaN sentinel before sparse-index remapping, fixing the illegal-memory-access path. A follow-up correctness defect remains: when DeepSelect sees any NaN with `abort_when_nan_found=False`, it writes only `output_idx[row, 0] = 0x3f3f3f3f` and returns. It leaves the other `index_topk - 1` output slots untouched.

The V4.1 sparse MQA path reuses caller-owned `col_indices_buffer` across steps. `SparseMQAIndexer.forward` clears `topk_indices_buffer`, but not that DeepSelect scratch. Thus #58215 maps the first sentinel to `-1`, while the other unwritten slots retain prior-row indices. Since those stale columns are normally in `[0, width)`, they pass the new bound and are remapped as real attention positions.

This is not a second OOB access: it is silent stale top-k selection after a NaN row.

## Source evidence

- vLLM calls DeepSelect with `abort_when_nan_found=False` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/indexer_topk.py`.
- The pinned DeepSelect source (`d96d33afe1fa`; current DeepSelect main has the same behavior) implements `take_action_when_have_nan` by writing only slot 0 and returning.
- V4.1 allocates `col_indices_buffer` once in `vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_indexer.py`; `vllm/model_executor/layers/sparse_mqa_indexer.py` does not reset it per forward.

## Proposed vLLM-side repair

Before calling DeepSelect, replace NaN sparse logits in rows with `end > topk` by `-inf` in place. DeepSelect then produces a complete top-k from finite candidate columns. Keep #58215's `c < width` remap bound as the final safety guard.

A post-sentinel refill is not sufficient: the selector never ranked the other slots. For an all-NaN row, this policy deterministically chooses valid `-inf`-tied candidate columns rather than using stale data.

## Regression

Extend `test_sparse_topk_remap_bounds_nan_rows` to prefill `col_indices` with a valid-looking poison value, insert NaNs in a row, and assert the remapped set equals:

```python
logits.nan_to_num(nan=-float("inf")).topk(topk, dim=-1).indices
```

The #58215-only implementation fails this test because the poison survives beyond slot 0.

## Observed serving impact

On a GB200 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash disaggregated lane, #58215 removed the IMA but changed speculative acceptance length by -3.39% in a controlled mount-only A/B, while raw sparse scoring remains faster per token. This issue identifies the missing contract handling that can change the selected set; the proposed repair still needs the described SM100 regression plus matched serving/accuracy validation before it is shipped.

## Duplicate-work check

Checked open PRs for `#58215`, `DeepSelect`, and `sparse indexer`; none addresses completion of unwritten DeepSelect output after a NaN. This is intentionally a follow-up to #58215, not a duplicate OOB-bound fix.

title: [RFC]: Enable libtorch-ABI-stable vLLM cuda wheels
body:
### Motivation.

PyTorch is building out a limited ABI through which custom ops writers can build extensions that build with one torch version and run on another. vLLM is an important part of the ecosystem that depends on torch. We'd like to help enable building vLLM wheels that would not be tied to a specific torch version to promote build system simplicity and general developer experience.

### Proposed Change.

As PyTorch increases our ABI surface, we'd love vLLM's collaboration in testing out our stable APIs. We've gone through the repo and gathered the following torch APIs that we are working to make stable. The hope is that once we have the stable versions of these ops, we can build vLLM cuda wheels in a libtorch stable manner, similar to what we did in FA3 here: https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/pull/1791

The APIs:
- [ ] Various TORCH_LIBRARY registrations [[link](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/torch_bindings.cpp)]
- [ ] at::Tag [[link](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/1c63a16b653d1f3f4260e862f01eaffed283c4c8/csrc/torch_bindings.cpp#L30)]
- [ ] Device stuff
    - [ ] torch::kDevice
    - [ ] at::Device
    - [ ] t.device().type()
    - [ ] Get_device
- [ ] SymInt [[link](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/torch_bindings.cpp#L304)]
    - We're wondering if we can replace these with ints and use Python meta functions to support compile
- [ ] Tensor[] [[link](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/torch_bindings.cpp#L780)] and Int[] [[link](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/torch_bindings.cpp#L747)]
- [ ] Various AT_DISPATCH macros [[link](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/dispatch_utils.h)]
    - [ ] AT_DISPATCH_SWITCH, AT_DISPATCH_CASE, AT_DISPATCH_BYTE_CASE
- [ ] at::get_num_threads
- [ ] at::cuda::OptionalCUDAGuard
- [ ] at::cuda::getCurrentCUDAStream()
- [ ] torch::from_blob
- [ ] torch::full
- [ ] tensor.index(torch::indexing::Slice(...))
- [ ] torch::empty(..., TensorOptions.device(...).dtype(...))
- [ ] tensor.sum(dim)
- [ ] Equivalent_scalar_type_v
- [ ] Tensor.const_data_ptr

Questions for vLLM maintainers:
1. How does the plan sound? Is libtorch ABI stability of interest?
2. Does the list of APIs seem conclusive? Did we miss any major APIs in our lookthrough?
3. Is there anything we can clarify?

### Feedback Period.

As we're seeking an open continuous collaboration, there's no real "deadline". That said, we think it would be feasible to support vLLM CUDA kernels by PyTorch 2.10 (branch cut is slotted for early December), so we'd like to get started on this as soon as possible.

### CC List.

@mikaylagawarecki @zou3519 @albanD

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [Performance]: MoE decode ~15% slower on SM12x since #56876 (DeepGEMM contiguous-layout alignment 128 instead of 64)
body:
### Report of performance regression

Since #56876 moved DeepGEMM to vllm-project/DeepGEMM `e1f418c2`, `get_theoretical_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout` returns 128 on SM12x. DeepGEMM 2.6.1 (`8b1392b9`) returned 64 when each expert gets at most 64 rows. The fork's SM120 port (vllm-project/DeepGEMM#4) left that rule unwired. vLLM pads the contiguous MoE layout with this alignment, so decode pads twice as many rows and the grouped GEMMs run with `BLOCK_M=128`.

DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, DFlash (7 speculative tokens), TP1, vLLM main 70fc359d (official cu130 aarch64 wheel). Server-side time per decode step:

| | 1 request | 16 requests |
|---|---|---|
| main | 56.6 ms | 173.7 ms |
| main + diff below | 50.2 ms | 146.5 ms |
| c81ace18 build (before #56876) | 50.5 ms | 149.0 ms |

With nsys at 16 requests, the MoE grouped GEMMs and the SiLU-mul/quant kernels account for 23.5 of the 23.7 ms difference. Greedy output is identical with and without the diff.

### Proposal to improve performance

Port the SM12x rule from deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#447 into vllm-project/DeepGEMM and bump the pin, or restore it in vLLM's wrapper. This is equivalent to the patch measured above:

```diff
--- a/vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py
+++ b/vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py
@@ -382,6 +382,13 @@ def get_theoretical_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout(
     _lazy_init()
     if _get_theoretical_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout_impl is None:
         return _missing()
+    if current_platform.is_device_capability_family(120):
+        # vllm-project/DeepGEMM returns 128 on SM12x; 2.6.1 used 64 when each
+        # expert gets at most 64 rows.
+        per_group_m = expected_m
+        if expected_m is not None and num_groups:
+            per_group_m = cdiv(expected_m, num_groups)
+        return 64 if per_group_m is not None and per_group_m <= 64 else 128
     if num_groups is None:
         return _get_theoretical_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout_impl(expected_m)
     if num_groups <= 0:
```

From reading the code only (not measured): on SM10x the fork returns a fixed 256 regardless of `expected_m`, so the alignment no longer shrinks below 128, where 2.6.1 went down to 32 for small per-expert M. Small-batch decode on B200/GB200 may be affected the same way.

I'm not planning to open a PR for this, so it's free for anyone to pick up.

title: vllm serve segfaults deterministically right after weight loading (single L4 GPU, V1 engine) — only avoided by VLLM_TRACE_FUNCTION=1
body:
### Description

`vllm serve` segfaults deterministically right after model weight
loading completes, during the internal profile run (before KV cache
size is computed) — on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU (Ada, SM 8.9), serving
`Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base` in bf16 with `--enforce-eager`.

The crash is 100% reproducible, always at the exact same point, and
survives every targeted configuration change I tried. The only thing
that avoids it is `VLLM_TRACE_FUNCTION=1`, which slows down execution
massively and produces a clean, healthy startup instead — suggesting a
race condition sensitive to real-time execution pacing, not a
configuration error.

### Environment

- vLLM versions tested: **0.20.2** and **0.22.0** (identical crash on
  both)
- GPU: 1x NVIDIA L4 (Ada Lovelace, SM 8.9) — Hugging Face Spaces
  `l4x1` hardware
- Base image: `nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04`
- Python: 3.11
- Torch: 2.11.0 (as resolved for vLLM 0.22.0)
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base`, dtype bf16
- Single GPU, `tensor_parallel_size=1` (no parallelism)

### Reproduction

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base \
    --enable-lora \
    --lora-modules dpo=<a private LoRA adapter repo> \
    --max-lora-rank 16 \
    --enforce-eager \
    --port 8000
```

(The crash also happens with `--enable-lora`/`--lora-modules`/
`--max-lora-rank` entirely removed — see "Ruled out" below.)

### Crash log (representative, vLLM 0.20.2)

```
(EngineCore pid=141) INFO [default_loader.py:384] Loading weights took 0.35 seconds
(EngineCore pid=141) INFO [punica_selector.py:20] Using PunicaWrapperGPU.
(EngineCore pid=141) INFO [gpu_model_runner.py:4879] Model loading took 3.26 GiB memory and 7.021560 seconds
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in _PyFunction_Vectorcall
  ... (all frames generic CPython interpreter frames, no native symbols)
```

### Crash log (vLLM 0.22.0, LoRA enabled — more detailed native trace this time)

Same crash point, but this run surfaces real native frames instead of
only generic Python ones, right after a new log line not present in
0.20.2 (`Using default LoRA kernel configs`):

```
(EngineCore pid=143) INFO [model_runner.py:295] Model loading took 3.26 GiB and 11.228786 seconds
(EngineCore pid=143) WARNING [utils.py:279] Using default LoRA kernel configs
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
  ...
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in pybind11::object pybind11::detail::object_api<pybind11::handle>::operator()<...>
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in torch::impl::dispatch::PythonKernelHolder::operator()(c10::OperatorHandle const&, c10::DispatchKeySet, std::vector<c10::IValue, ...>*)
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in c10::Dispatcher::callBoxed(c10::OperatorHandle const&, std::vector<c10::IValue, ...>*) const [clone .isra.0]
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in torch::jit::invokeOperatorFromPython(...)
  File "<unknown>", line 0, in torch::jit::_get_operation_for_overload_or_packet(...)
  ...
```

Note the LoRA-kernel-config log line above turned out to be a red
herring — see "Ruled out" (LoRA was later excluded with a clean test
on this same 0.22.0 build).

### What I ruled out (each tested independently, in a real deployment, same crash every time unless noted)

1. **`VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0`** — no effect (this variable
   only applies to the offline `LLM()` path, not `vllm serve`,
   confirmed by reading `vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py`:
   `make_async_mp_client` is called unconditionally for the async
   server).
2. **Container running as root vs. explicit non-root UID 1000** —
   fixed a real permissions issue (Triton JIT cache resolution under
   `$HOME`), kept as a real fix, but did **not** affect this crash.
3. **LoRA / Punica** — tested with `--enable-lora` fully removed, on
   *both* 0.20.2 and 0.22.0. Identical crash both times, with no
   `PunicaWrapperGPU`/LoRA-kernel log lines at all. Not the cause.
4. **Attention backend** — `--attention-backend FLASHINFER` instead of
   the default FlashAttention2. Confirmed active via log
   (`Using AttentionBackendEnum.FLASHINFER backend.`). Identical
   crash.
5. **`--no-async-scheduling`** — confirmed active via
   `non-default args` log (`'async_scheduling': False`). Identical
   crash.
6. **Fixed startup delay** — added `sleep 20` before `vllm serve` to
   rule out the GPU/driver context not being fully stabilized right
   after a fresh container/GPU allocation. Identical crash.
7. **vLLM version** — 0.20.2 → 0.22.0, identical crash (0.22.0's
   `torch==2.11.0` pin was verified compatible with Python 3.11 before
   testing). A further jump to 0.28.0 was not reachable: its resolved
   torch dependency requires Python 3.12 (`sys.get_int_max_str_digits`,
   added in 3.12), unrelated to this bug.

### The one thing that "fixes" it (but isn't usable)

Setting `VLLM_TRACE_FUNCTION=1` (traces every Python function call,
documented as a >100x slowdown) results in a **complete, healthy
startup** — model loads, LoRA adapter loads, KV cache is sized, the
OpenAI-compatible server comes up and serves `/health` successfully.
This is not viable for real traffic due to the slowdown, but strongly
suggests a race condition whose outcome depends on real-time execution
pacing, rather than a deterministic logic bug tied to any single flag
above.

### Additional environment note

I could not test a different GPU architecture as an additional data
point: switching this same Space to `a10g-large` hardware left the
container stuck indefinitely at boot (no logs at all beyond the
platform's own startup banner, not even reaching vLLM's own startup
banner), reproduced on two separate restarts. I reverted to `l4x1`
rather than continue debugging what looks like an unrelated
provisioning issue on that hardware class, so I cannot say whether
this bug is Ada-architecture-specific.

Happy to provide the full uncut logs for either vLLM version, or run
further targeted diagnostics, if useful.
