title: [RFC]: Increase vLLM Review Capacity with a Reviewer Role
body:
## Motivation

vLLM’s contribution volume exceeds its available review and triage capacity, creating a massive PR backlog. To help address this backlog and stem its future growth, we propose a **Reviewer** role to expand the community of trusted reviewers who take ownership of triage and initial review, helping authors bring their PRs up to vLLM’s standards. Today, much of that responsibility falls on committers, who must balance review with implementation, architectural decisions, releases, and maintenance.

The growing volume of low-quality AI-generated contributions (“AI slop”) compounds this problem, increasing the effort required to identify worthwhile changes and bring them up to project standards. The Reviewer title also recognizes review as a valuable contribution and establishes a clearer path toward committership.

## The Reviewer Role

Reviewers take ownership of triage and initial review, helping contributors bring their PRs up to vLLM’s standards. This includes understanding the problem, evaluating the proposed solution, examining correctness and validation, and working with authors to resolve concerns. Reviewers help address common issues that consume review capacity, including unnecessary complexity, poorly scoped changes, overspecified tests, unjustified modifications to core code, and missing performance measurements or accuracy evaluations. Addressing these issues is especially valuable as AI-generated contributions increase.

Reviewer status formally recognizes contributors’ review work and the trust they have earned within the project. Following [Kubernetes’ reviewer/approver model](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/b8ce3416617273bfb8611b18b4cd8412893e44db/community-membership.md), authors are expected to address reviewer feedback by making changes or responding with an explanation before requesting final committer review. Outstanding concerns must be resolved, or explicitly adjudicated by a committer, before the PR is merged. Reviewers should involve relevant committers when questions require their input.

The formal title signals to contributors that reviewer feedback is part of the project’s acceptance process and must be addressed. It also signals to other committers that they can rely on reviewers’ judgment within the scope of the review they performed.

Reviewers can:

- Review PRs and provide a recognized approval or request changes.  
- Trigger CI when a contribution is ready for evaluation.  
- Escalate design questions to the appropriate committer and SIG.  
- Triage PRs/issues and apply appropriate labels; flagging potentially important PRs that should receive expedited committer attention.  
- Close duplicate PRs/issues to cut down noise and focus effort on the most promising contributions.  
- Flag PRs that are ready for committer review, approval, and merge.

Reviewers cannot:

- Merge PRs into main themselves, even when approved and CI is green.

A completed reviewer pass should give the committer a useful starting point: what was checked, what evidence is available, and what still needs committer attention. Ideally, committer review should be minimal at this point, mostly an LGTM and final approval, with substantive concerns already addressed during reviewer-led triage and initial review.

Substantive requests for changes must be resolved before merge, either through revisions or an explicit resolution by a committer. Authors may ask for clarification or escalate disagreements; reviewer status does not make every preference a requirement. Reviewer approval signals readiness for final consideration. It does not replace committer review or guarantee acceptance.

## Assigning Reviewers

A list of active reviewers will be made public in [https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/community/reviewers](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/community/reviewers) and will include recommendations on their areas of expertise/knowledge. Reviewers should self-assign PRs they are actively reviewing and publicly coordinate with other reviewers in \#pr-reviews. 

## Appointment and Development

Candidates should demonstrate a sustained record of useful reviews, sound engineering judgment, constructive communication, and familiarity with vLLM’s contribution standards. Deep ownership of a subsystem is not required. A reviewer should be nominated by 2 committers from different organizations. Committers should post in \#committers when nominating reviewers.

Before being nominated a general rule of thumb (not a hard requirement) are the reviewer should have either 15 merged PRs and have reviewed\* 30 PRs OR have reviewed\* 45 PRs.

\* “Reviewed” implies the reviewer gave a substantive review and the PR went on to some kind of resolution (merged or closed)

New reviewers should receive feedback and mentorship from committers. A private Slack channel will be set up to facilitate communication between Reviewers and Committers, including review questions, feedback, and coordination on PRs.

First serving as a reviewer will become the standard path for new committer appointments. This establishes demonstrated review service as part of the path to merge authority. While this is not a hard requirement and there may be exceptions we do consider this the standard and preferred path.

## Rollout and Evaluation

Start with a small cohort of trusted reviewers working across the project (initially \~50, potentially scaling up to 2x active committers).

Things to assess:

- Time to first substantive review and time waiting for final committer review.  
- Review quality, i.e. committer effort required to bring reviewed contributions to a final decision.  
- CI queue pressure.  
- Backlog size and age, distinguishing merged PRs from closed or withdrawn PRs.

Success is a sustained increase in effective review capacity: contributions receive useful feedback sooner, review responsibility is distributed across more trusted contributors, and the backlog declines without compromising quality or overloading reviewers and CI.

Community members should have access to a directory of which reviewers to reach out to for different topics, to enable them collaborate effectively on slack channels such as \#pr-reviews

## Precedents

Several established projects distribute review responsibilities beyond contributors with final acceptance or merge authority:

- [**Kubernetes**](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/community-membership.md#reviewer) distinguishes Reviewers, who assess contribution quality and correctness, from Approvers, who authorize acceptance.  
- [**containerd**](https://github.com/containerd/.project/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md#reviewers) has explicit Reviewer and Committer tiers. Reviewers’ LGTMs count toward merge requirements, but reviewers do not have write access. Reviewer service is part of the path toward committership.  
- [**Python / CPython**](https://devguide.python.org/triage/triage-team/) has a formal Triage Team whose responsibilities include reviewing PRs, assisting contributors, and involving core developers. Its stated purpose is to provide timely feedback and reduce core-developer workload.

### Proposed Change.

## Implementation

The implementation must give reviewer decisions meaningful visibility while keeping final acceptance and merging with committers.

### Option A \[Selected\]: Native GitHub reviews with restricted merging

Give Reviewers Write access, and restrict updates to protected branches to the Committer team and authorized bots. This gives reviewer feedback native GitHub review authority, including blocking requests for changes under the configured review rules.

This option uses GitHub’s existing review interface without requiring a bot to recognize reviewer approvals. It does grant broader write privileges, including on unprotected branches. All relevant branches and merge paths must therefore be covered by the restrictions, and the configuration must be verified before rollout. GitHub documents these capabilities in its [repository role permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-repository-roles/repository-roles-for-an-organization) and [branch protection rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches).


<details>

<summary>Other options considered</summary>
### Option B: Triage access with a bot-managed review check

Give Reviewers Triage access and use a bot to recognize reviews from the designated Reviewer team. The bot would publish a named status check, such as “Reviewer approval,” and track unresolved requests for changes.

The bot would make Reviewer approvals visible as a readiness signal without requiring them for merge. It would separately track unresolved Reviewer requests for changes so those concerns must be resolved or explicitly adjudicated by a Committer. A bot-generated check would not change the permissions or appearance of the native GitHub review. This option preserves the absence of repository write access but requires automation that handles team membership, updated commits, dismissed reviews, outstanding objections, and explicit committer resolutions correctly.

#### Review Automation Options

##### Prow

[Kubernetes’ Prow](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prow) provides an established command model:

- `/cc @username`: request review from a contributor.  
- `/assign @username`: assign responsibility for a PR.  
- `/lgtm`: record that a change looks good following review.  
- `/lgtm cancel`: withdraw that review signal.  
- `/approve`: record final acceptance by an authorized approver.  
- `/hold`: prevent automatic merging while an outstanding concern is resolved.

For vLLM, `/lgtm` could represent a trusted Reviewer or Committer’s completed review, while `/approve` would remain restricted to Committers. Committers could perform both steps directly. Prow can also translate native GitHub approval and request-changes reviews into LGTM label changes.

Prow’s default authorization does not exactly match this proposal: `/lgtm` is generally available to repository collaborators, while `/approve` uses OWNERS files.

##### Mergeable

[Mergeable](https://mergeable.readthedocs.io/en/latest/validators/approval.html) can react to native GitHub reviews through `pull_request_review.*`, count approvals from designated teams, and publish a review check. Its [approval validator](https://github.com/mergeability/mergeable/blob/master/lib/validators/approvals.js) filters reviews by team membership or username without requiring write access, making it a candidate for recognizing Triage-only Reviewer approvals. Reviewers could use GitHub’s normal Approve and Request changes actions, with a passing check signaling readiness for committer review. 

##### A lightweight GitHub App or GitHub Actions workflow

Custom automation could recognize native reviews or a small command set from explicit Reviewer and Committer teams, publish review status, and integrate with existing CI labels and triggers. This offers the most direct fit for Option B but makes vLLM responsible for maintaining the implementation.

</details>

### CI access

The implementation should verify the behavior of labels and CI triggers and build on existing controls where possible. CI access should allow reviewers to unblock ready contributions without routinely involving a committer. Reviewers should assess readiness before triggering expensive jobs and avoid unnecessary reruns. Faster review may increase CI demand even if incoming PR volume stays constant. The rollout should monitor queue times and resource use.

title: [Feature]: Structured request_id in logs and inclusion in error logs
body:
# Structured request_id in logs and inclusion in error logs

When sending a request with the `x-request-id` header, vLLM logs an entry like:

```
[2025-11-14 13:57:07] [INFO] [vllm.v1.engine.async_llm] Added request cmpl-833171a7b8c84e5eb20408b3e4fe2377
```

This is quite useful for traceability, but it currently has two limitations.

## 1. `request_id` is not available as a structured logging field

The `request_id` appears only inside the log message text, not as a dedicated log record field.
This prevents using it in structured logging formats such as:

```json
{
    "formatters": {
        "vllm": {
            "class": "vllm.logging_utils.NewLineFormatter",
            "datefmt": "%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
            "format": "%(levelname)s %(asctime)s %(filename)s:%(lineno)d %(request_id)s %(message)s"
        }
    }
}
```

Since `request_id` is not part of the log record, any formatter referencing it fails.

Adding `request_id` as an optional field in the logger would enable proper log correlation and integration with observability tools.

## 2. Error logs do not include the `request_id`

If the request is valid, vLLM logs the “Added request …” line containing the `request_id`, as stated above. 

However, if the request fails before being accepted—e.g., invalid JSON, exceeding max context length, or other early validation errors—**the error logs do not include the `request_id`**, even when the header is present.

Example:

```
[2025-11-18 11:37:57] [ERROR] [vllm.entrypoints.openai.serving_chat] ValueError: This model's maximum context length is 8192 tokens. However, your request has 54732 input tokens. Please reduce the length of the input messages.
```

This makes end-to-end tracing difficult precisely in the cases where correlation is most needed.

# Summary:

* Expose `request_id` as a structured logging attribute.
* Include `request_id` in error logs, even when the request fails early.
* Maintain backward compatibility.

These changes would improve observability and make vLLM easier to operate in production environments.

Thank you for the great work on vLLM. It’s an outstanding project!

title: `NixlPushMode` Roadmap - Reliability Issue Inventory
body:
List of planned enhancements and fixes for the `NixlPushModeConnector`, aimed at solidifying the implementation for large-scale operational deployments and for use behind an orchestration layer (llm-d / Dynamo), bringing its reliability and failure-handling to parity with the mature pull-mode connector.
Will track respective PRs here.

**Priority:**
- 🔴 **P0** = blocks primetime
- 🟠 **P1** = high
- 🟡 **P2** = medium
- ⚪ **P3** = low / optional

**Summary:** 🔴 **4× P0**, 🟠 **4× P1**, 🟡 **4× P2**, ⚪ **2× P3**

**P0 blockers:** 🔴 **C3, C1** (silent corruption), 🔴 **L1** (no liveness loop), 🔴 **S2** (head-of-line handshake)

## Correctness (can produce wrong / torn KV)

| ID | Priority | PR(s) | Issue | Evidence | Impact |
|----|----------|-------|-------|----------|--------|
| C3 | 🔴 P0 | https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48758 | Missing `_apply_prefix_caching`: on a **partial** prefix-cache hit, D registers only its uncached suffix (`get_unhashed_block_ids_all_groups`) but the WRITE aligns via a `min`-length **front-trim**, sending P's prefix blocks into D's suffix slots. Pull end-trims via `_apply_prefix_caching`. | `push_worker.py:634-640` vs `base_worker.py:2202,2226`; `push_scheduler.py:172`; safe paths `push_scheduler.py:161-164` | Silent KV corruption on any partial prefix hit |
| C1 | 🔴 P0 | ☐ | D aborts after PUSH_REG sent: D frees blocks immediately (`delay_free=False`) while P still holds the pending reg and later WRITEs into D's freed/reallocated blocks. No cancel signal, no delay-free guard, no validity token. | `push_scheduler.py:250-259`; `push_worker.py:268,660` | Silent cross-request corruption |
| C2 | 🟠 P1 | ☐ | Partial multi-rank WRITE failure: per-rank loop tracks only successful handles; D waits for `pp_size * producers_per_consumer` notifs and never reaches the count. | `push_worker.py:547-580,720-725` | Request hangs + partially-written KV |
| C4 | 🟡 P2 | ☐ | Suffix-stripped fallback matching (`get_base_request_id`) returns the *first* base-id match with no recency check; a stale reg/blocks entry from a resubmit/retry sharing the base id can mis-pair. | `utils.py:66-68`; `push_worker.py:351-357,372-374` | Wrong pairing |

## Failure detection / liveness

| ID | Priority | PR(s) | Issue | Evidence | Impact |
|----|----------|-------|-------|----------|--------|
| L1 | 🔴 P0 | ☐ | No closed-loop D recv lease: heartbeats are one-way D→P only, the only timer is a static 480s TTL (`push_registration_timeout`→`decoder_kv_blocks_ttl`), and the watchdog that fires neither fails the request nor cleans the worker's `_recving_metadata`. Needs a bidirectional lease-extension that actually terminates a stuck D request. | `push_scheduler.py:317-326`; `base_worker.py:2038-2057,2145`; `base_scheduler.py:154-158` | Dead-P requests hang up to 480s and aren't cleanly failed |
| F5 | ⚪ P3 | ☐ | Failed WRITE is dropped, never retried: matched pair is popped before the WRITE and the scheduler feed is one-shot; self-poll only retries *unmatched* blocks, not *failed* WRITEs. | `push_worker.py:215-217,263-268,672-688` | Transient WRITE error = permanent request failure |

## Writer thread robustness

| ID | Priority | PR(s) | Issue | Evidence | Impact |
|----|----------|-------|-------|----------|--------|
| W2 | 🟡 P2 | ☐ | Unsupervised writer (merges former W1): `except Exception: ...continuing` hot-spins on a persistent error; no liveness/restart/health signal. If it wedges (or dies on BaseException), the main thread keeps enqueuing to queues nobody drains. | `push_worker.py:240-241`; no `is_alive`/restart | Silent rank-wide push hang if writer wedges |
| W3 | 🟡 P2 | ☐ | No in-flight WRITE drain on shutdown: `join(timeout=2)` then unconditionally release all handles; not tied to `--shutdown-timeout`. | `push_worker.py:134-146` | Abandoned WRITEs → D timeouts on scale-down |

## Scale / connection management

| ID | Priority | PR(s) | Issue | Evidence | Impact |

Should move to a background executor. | `push_worker.py:404,450`; `base_worker.py:604` | One slow/dead D stalls the whole rank |
| S1 | 🟠 P1 | https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50234 | P-side D-engine state never evicted: `_ensure_d_handshake` stores `_remote_agents` but never sets `_engine_last_active`, which `_evict_stale_engines` iterates. | `push_worker.py:473` vs `base_worker.py:854,2397-2426` | Unbounded growth / OOM under D churn (rollouts, autoscale) |

title: [RFC]: Pluggable KV connector metrics on the Rust frontend via connector metrics descriptor
body:
<!-- proposed title: [RFC]: Pluggable KV connector metrics on the Rust frontend via connector metrics descriptor -->

### Motivation.

[vllm-project/vllm#52755](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52755) added Rust frontend Prometheus metrics for **Nixl** and **Mooncake**. But other KV connectors still have no metrics on that frontend, including the in-tree **Offloading**, **HF3FS**, and **HiSparse** connectors and all **third-party** connectors.

On the Python frontend this already works without hardcoding each connector: a shared plugin asks the configured connector for its metrics, and the connector owns registration and observation. If we repeat the Nixl/Mooncake pattern in Rust, adding a typed decode and observe branch for each connector inside the frontend, it does not scale, and it cannot cover connectors whose code never lands in the vLLM tree.

The Rust frontend cannot reuse the Python plugin path, because it runs in a separate process from EngineCore and cannot import connector Python classes. Connector stats reach it only as a field in the scheduler stats sent from EngineCore. Stats from any connector other than Nixl and Mooncake currently have no matching Rust type and are dropped.

What is missing is a way for KV connectors other than Nixl and Mooncake, both in-tree and out-of-tree, to expose their metrics on the Rust frontend, without the frontend adding code for each connector. The Python frontend already has this property.

### Proposed Change.

This RFC proposes a generic way to observe KV connector Prometheus metrics on the Rust frontend, for connectors other than Nixl and Mooncake, including the in-tree builtins (Offloading, HF3FS, HiSparse) and third-party connectors. Nixl and Mooncake keep their existing typed path unchanged.

We introduce a **metrics descriptor**: a small, self-describing document that a connector attaches to its stats. It carries what the Rust frontend needs to register Prometheus metrics: metric names, types, help text, histogram buckets, and where each metric's values sit in the stats payload. When the Rust frontend is enabled, the first stats payload from a connector includes the descriptor, and Rust registers the metrics once. Later payloads carry only values, which Rust records into the registered metrics. `GET /metrics` only renders the Rust-side registry and never calls into connector Python. On the Python frontend the descriptor is not attached, so that path has no extra cost.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  EC[EngineCore connector stats] --> RF[Rust frontend]
  RF --> D{Connector?}
  D -->|Nixl / Mooncake| T[Existing typed path]
  D -->|Other| S[Descriptor-driven path]
  S --> P1[First payload carries descriptor: register once]
  S --> P2[Later payloads carry values only: record]
  P1 --> P[Prometheus /metrics]
  P2 --> P
  T --> P
```

#### How the Rust frontend handles descriptors

The Rust frontend keeps each registered descriptor under its `connector_id`. When a payload with a descriptor arrives, it registers that connector's metrics and records the values in the same payload. Later value-only payloads are matched to the registered descriptor: a single connector's stats map to its one descriptor, and under MultiConnector each child's stats are matched by the child's class name. If stats arrive from a connector that has never sent a descriptor (for example, a connector that has not adopted this mechanism), the frontend logs one warning and ignores them. It does not fail, and other connectors' metrics are unaffected.

#### What ships in vLLM

vLLM ships the generic Rust-side registration and recording, a shared Python helper that attaches the descriptor only on the Rust frontend and only once, and descriptors for the in-tree Offloading, HF3FS, and HiSparse connectors. The builtins derive their descriptors from the same definitions their Python Prom metrics use, rather than from a separately maintained file. Third-party descriptors live in the third-party packages.

#### How third-party KV connectors adopt this mechanism

A connector that already reports Prometheus metrics on the Python frontend (via `KVConnectorStats` and `build_prom_metrics()`) needs only a few additions to expose the same metrics on the Rust frontend. The in-tree builtins serve as references: **HiSparse** (`hisparse/stats.py`) is the smallest example, **HF3FS** covers histograms, and **Offloading** derives the descriptor from existing metric metadata.

**1. A single source of metric definitions.** Each metric is declared once, with its Prometheus name, type, help text, and (for histograms) buckets. Both the Python Prom metrics and the descriptor are built from that declaration. HiSparse uses a small tuple table; Offloading reuses its existing metadata classes. This avoids a second hand-maintained copy that can drift.

**2. Information Rust cannot infer.** Python Prom code knows how to apply each value because it is code. Rust sees only the descriptor, so each metric entry also has to state:

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| `name`, `type`, `documentation`, `buckets` | Same as the Python Prom metric (`type` is `counter`, `gauge`, or `histogram`) |
| `samples_path` | The key in the connector's stats dict (`KVConnectorStats.data`) that holds this metric's values |
| `sample_kind` | How the values are applied: add one integer, add the sum of a list, add a float, set a gauge, or observe each list element into a histogram |

The descriptor also carries a `connector_id`, which should be the connector class name; MultiConnector uses the same name as the key when nesting child stats.

**3. Attaching the descriptor during serialization.** The connector's stats class returns its data from `to_dict()` through the shared helper, and strips the descriptor key when stats are rebuilt from the wire (`__post_init__`). The helper handles gating: it attaches the descriptor only when the Rust frontend is enabled, and only on the first emit. No new RPC, environment variable, or config file is required.

**4. Guaranteeing a first emit.** Rust can register the metrics only after it has seen one payload that carries the descriptor. A connector that may stay silent for a long time after startup should emit one zero-valued snapshot early (HiSparse does this on its first empty poll).

**5. Verification.** With `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1` and some traffic, the connector's metric names should appear on `/metrics`, with values matching a Python frontend run.

One current limit: every metric must be declared in the descriptor up front, so a metric that a connector only creates later at runtime has to be included in the descriptor from the start.

### Any Other Things.

#### Non-goals

- Moving Nixl and Mooncake to the descriptor path. They keep their existing typed path.
- Printing connector stats in the Rust frontend's periodic log line, as the Python frontend does today.
- Labels derived from payload contents. Metric labels stay fixed (per engine), so connectors cannot add arbitrary label values at runtime.

#### Implementation

Implementation, tests, and end-to-end results: #58563

#### AI assistance

This RFC was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed and revised by the author, who is responsible for the design.

title: [Feature]: Parser cache for streaming chat derender and stable tool call IDs on retried calls
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for work deferred from the streaming derender RFC #47161 and PR #50550: server side parser state for streaming chat derender, and keeping tool call IDs stable when a chunk is retried.

#### Where things stand

With a reasoning or tool parser configured, streaming chat derender keeps nothing on the server. Each chunk builds a fresh parser, replays the history the client echoes back in `stream_state` (`output_token_ids`, split by `output_chunk_lens`) through `parse_delta`, then feeds the new chunk (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat_stream_parsed`). Any replica can serve any chunk and the client carried state is the only source of truth.

The price is replay. It's O(n²) `parse_delta` calls over a generation and O(n³) character work for parsers that re-scan accumulated text (Hermes tool call JSON, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning). The "Streaming cost" section of `derenderer.md` documents this. @shimib measured it on 1×A100-40G with Qwen3-8B and the hermes + qwen3 parsers (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56851#issuecomment-5685698033): ~9× the in-process CPU at matched load, +15% E2E p50 on multi-thousand-token reasoning outputs and a saturated tier under concurrent parsed streams with the default `renderer_num_workers=1`.

Latency sensitive P/D goes to #56851 where the parser lives with the request on the decode pool and there's no replay. This issue covers the consumers that keep using streaming derender: RL, batch and gateways that own postprocessing.

#### 1. Parser cache

An LRU of live `Parser` instances on the derenderer, keyed by `(request_id, choice_index)`, as the "Future" note in #47161 describes. Each entry records how many chunks its parser has consumed. On a hit where that matches `len(stream_state.output_chunk_lens)`, skip replay and feed only the new chunk, so compute drops to O(delta). Anything else falls back to full replay: first chunk, eviction, a chunk that landed on another replica, a retry or out of order input. `stream_state` stays authoritative, so there's no protocol change and a hit has to produce exactly what replay would.

Design questions:

- **What a hit must check.** `request_id` comes from the client (`generate_chunk.request_id`), so the key alone can't be trusted. A hit needs to confirm the cached parser saw the same `prompt_token_ids`, `chat_request` and output history, e.g. with a digest stored in the entry. Otherwise one stream can pick up another stream's parser state.
- **Memory bounds and eviction.** Bound by entry count and TTL, and evict on the finish chunk. Streams abandoned midway never send a finish chunk, so the TTL has to cover them.
- **Concurrency.** Parsing runs on the renderer executor's thread pool and a retry can race the original call. Taking the entry out of the cache for the duration of the call and putting it back at its new position keeps two calls from sharing a parser.
- **Routing.** Without session affinity, a stream's chunks spread across N replicas and the hit rate drops to about 1/N. We should document routing on `request_id` for deployments that want the cache to pay off.
- **Default.** I'd make it opt in and off by default, so a stateless render tier stays the default.
- **What to cache.** A bare `Parser` or the shared per choice `ChatStreamProcessor` (#57572) if that lands first.

#### 2. Tool call ID stability on retried calls

Raised by @sagearc in the #50550 review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913963783).

Within one stream, IDs are already stable. `stream_state.last_tool_call_ids` pins the ID emitted for each tool call index, so replay never changes an ID the client saw on an earlier chunk. The gap is the chunk where a tool call's ID first appears. With the default `tool_call_id_type` (`random`), `make_tool_call_id` returns `chatcmpl-tool-{random_uuid()}`. If the client retries that chunk with the same `stream_state` (lost response, timeout, retry on another replica), the retry gets a new ID. If the first response reached anyone anyway, the same call now has two IDs. Rerunning a whole stream over the same generate output gives new IDs too. `kimi_k2` IDs (`functions.{name}:{idx}`) are derived from the input, so they aren't affected.

Options:

- **The cache remembers the IDs it assigned** per `(request_id, choice_index, tool call index)`. This only helps on a hit, on the same replica and within the TTL.
- **Derive the ID from the request**, e.g. a hash of `request_id`, `choice_index` and the tool call index. It's stateless, so it works on any replica and could also cover the batch path. But `request_id` is client supplied, so two requests that reuse one would share tool call IDs and it changes what `random` means for `tool_call_id_type`.
- **Document it as a limitation.** A client that retries a chunk treats the retried response as replacing the first one.

#### Done when

- [ ] Parser cache design agreed here (hit check, bounds, concurrency, routing, default)
- [ ] Decision on tool call ID stability for retried calls
- [ ] Cache implemented with tests showing identical output with the cache on and off over the chunked path (plain, reasoning, tool, reasoning + tool, a multi-token chunk, a finish only chunk), including forced evictions midstream
- [ ] Benchmarked on @shimib's setup with and without the cache
- [ ] "Streaming cost" in `derenderer.md` updated

### Alternatives

- **Serialize parser state into `stream_state`.** Dropped. Parsers hold internals we can't cheaply round trip (`prev_tool_call_arr`, `current_tool_id`, `streamed_args_for_tool`, engine lexer buffers) and #32713 was closed as not planned.
- **Parse on the decode pool (#56851).** This is the answer for latency sensitive P/D. It doesn't help consumers that want a stateless render tier or do their own postprocessing.
- **Keep replay only.** Size `renderer_num_workers` for concurrent parsed streams and accept the cost. That's where things are after #50550.
- **Bidirectional streaming derender.** Suggested by @andylolu2. One stream per request holds the parser, so there's no cache, hit check, TTL or routing affinity. It needs a new streaming endpoint (WebSocket or gRPC) and a client change, so it doesn't replace the cache for existing clients. See https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57571#issuecomment-5764095680 for more details.

### Additional context

- RFC #47161, "Parser state: replay (no opaque serialization)"
- PR #50550 review threads from @sagearc:
  - shared `ChatStreamProcessor`: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913908193
  - retaining parser state per stream: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913925664
  - tool call ID stability on retries: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913963783
- Replay benchmark: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56851#issuecomment-5685698033
- Shared per choice `ChatStreamProcessor` for chat serving and derender: #57572
- Batch derender discards the parser's tool call ID: tracked under #42729
- #32713 (unified parser / serializable parser state, closed as not planned)

cc @sagearc @chaunceyjiang @shimib @bbrowning
